div.p: The Great Horse of the Emperor Domitian What mass is this, doubled by the colossus set upon it, that stands embracing the Latin Forum? Did the work flow down from heaven, complete? Or was the figure forged in Sicilian furnaces and left, when it was done, wearied Steropes and Brontes behind? Or did Pallas's hands fashion you for us such, Germanicus, as the Rhine and the towering house of the astonished Dacian lately beheld you, holding the reins in hand? Now let Fame, that of old admired through the ages the famous name of the Dardanian horse, admire this one—the horse for whom Dindymon was thinned at its sacred summit and Ide stripped of branches: him neither Pergamum could have taken in, with its walls breached, nor boys and unwed girls together in mingled crowd, nor Aeneas himself, nor great Hector, lead within! Add that the one was harmful and embraced the savage Achaeans; this one a gentle rider commends. It delights us to gaze on his face, blended with the marks of war yet wearing serene peace, nor would you think it greater than the truth: equal his form and grace, equal his dignity. Not higher does the Thracian war-horse bear Mars when his arms are spent, and proud he is of the mighty weight, and, seized in no slow course near the rivers, he steams and drives Strymon before him with his huge breath. A site to match the work: on this side the Julian halls open their welcoming threshold; on that, the lofty palace of warlike Paulus rises; behind, the Father; and with kindly face Concord looks on. But you yourself, your lofty head ringed with the clear air, outshine the temples, and seem to be gazing out to see whether a new Palatine rises more beautiful, the flames defied, or whether the Trojan fire keeps watch with silent torch, and Vesta now commends her tested handmaids. Your right hand forbids battle; your left the Tritonian maid does not weigh down, holding out before it the neck of severed Medusa: as if with goads she spurs the horse on; nor anywhere is there a sweeter seat chosen for the goddess, not even, Father, if you yourself held it. A breast that could unfold the cares of the world, and one to which Temese gave itself, drained of all its ore; a cloak hangs loose down your back; your side, with sword at rest, is unafraid—great as the blade with which Orion threatens on winter nights and frightens the stars. But the steed, mimicking the bearing and spirit of horses, lifts his airy face and threatens to gallop; his neck stands stiff with bristling mane, and living force runs through his shoulders, and his flanks, broad enough to bear such mighty spurs, lie open; in place of turf upon the empty ground a bronze hoof covers the hair of captive Rhine. At this sight Adrastus's Arion would have shuddered, and Cyllarus, son of Leda, looking on it from his nearby shrine, takes fright. This horse will never change his master's reins, forever bound to the bridle, and will serve one star alone! The ground scarcely suffices, and the earth, pressed beneath such weight, pants below; nor with iron or bronze: they labour under the genius of the place, though an eternal foundation hold it, which could have carried the summit of a mountain heaped above and stood up hardened by the knee of sky-bearing Atlas. Nor did long delays draw the work out: the very presence of the god's own form delights the labour, and the youth, intent upon the task, marvel that hands can do so much; the lofty engine clatters with the blows: a continuous din goes through the seven peaks of Mars and outdoes the wandering murmurs of great Rome. The guardian of the place himself—whose hallowed chasm and famous pool preserve a memorable name— when he heard the countless ringing of the bronze, and the Forum bellow under the harsh hammering, lifts his bristling face from its sacred squalor and his head, venerable with its well-earned oak. And first he took fright at the great form and the flashing light of the greater horse, and three times in alarm he plunged his towering neck into the pool—then, glad at the sight of the patron, said: 'Hail, offspring and begetter of the great gods, power heard of by me from far off! Now happy is my pool, now venerable, since I am granted to know you near and to gaze on your immortal radiance from a neighbouring seat, I who once, sole founder and discoverer, brought safety to Romulus's city. You tame Jove's wars, you the battles of the Rhine, you civil wickedness, you the mountain slow to its treaty, in a long war. But had our age given birth to you, you would have tried, where I dared not, to go down into the deep pool; yet Rome would have held your reins.' Let the horse give way that stands against the temple of Latian Dione in the seat of Caesar's forum—the one you, Lysippus, are said to have dared to make for the Pellaean leader, and which then bore the face of Caesar on its wondering neck—scarcely with weary eye could you survey how long the look down upon this one from that. Who is so untaught as not to say, once he has seen them both, that the horses differ as much as those who ride them? This work fears neither rain-bearing winters nor Jove's threefold fire, nor the marshalled storms of Aeolus's prison, nor the delays of the years: it shall stand while earth and pole endure, while there is a Roman day. Here too, under the silent night, when heavenly things are pleased by earthly, your kin, leaving heaven behind, shall glide down and mingle kisses close beside, and into your embrace shall come son and brother and father and sister: one neck shall give a place to all those stars. Enjoy forever this gift of the people and the great senate. Apelles's wax would long to portray you, and the aged Athenian of Elean Jove would have wished to set you, his likeness, in a new temple, and gentle Tarentum would have wished your face, and harsh Rhodes, scorning Phoebus, would prefer your eyes that imitate the starry flames; may you surely love the earth, and the temples we dedicate to you inhabit yourself; nor let heaven's court delight you, and may you, glad, see your descendants offer incense to this gift.

Glaucias, the favourite of Atedius Melior What solace can I bring you, Melior, for your foster-child snatched away, when, shameless, before the pyre and the embers still alive I begin? Even now the wound gapes, weeping, from broken veins, and the slippery path of a great gash lies open, while I cruelly already lay songs and healing words upon it. You would rather have beatings of the breast and the brave lamentings, and you hate the lyre and turn away with a deaf ear. Untimely I sing: sooner would the tigress, her young driven off, and the lions, bereaved, be willing to hear me, nor, if the threefold song of the Sicilian maiden should flow, or the lyre understood by woods and beasts, would it soothe your mad groans; in your breast there stands frantic grief, and your heart barks at the touch laid upon it. No one forbids you: sate yourself on your ills, and tame your sick sorrow by giving it free rein. Is the pleasure of weeping now fulfilled, and are you now, wearied, not unwilling at a friend's prayers? May I now sing? Behold, even my songs swim with tears in the very mouth, and sad blottings fall upon the words. For I myself with you led out the solemnities of the black procession and the crime that the City watched, and the boy's bier, and I saw the savage heaps of condemned incense and the weeping soul above its own funeral, and you, surpassing the groans of fathers and the arms of mothers, embracing the pyre and ready to drink in the fire, I scarcely held, a comrade like to you, and gave offence by holding you. And now, alas, with the fillets and the glory of my brow undone, an ill-omened poet, I beat my breast turned in grief with you upon the lyre. But you, my comrade and partner in sorrow, if I have deserved it and have felt a share of your mourning, now suffer me, gently, I pray. In the very thunderbolt the fathers heard me; I beside the tombs, when mothers poured out their grief and pious sons, sang consolations, and to myself, when I bewailed my own loss at his fire— who, O Nature!—my father; nor do I, stern, forbid you to mourn, but compare our groans, and let us weep alike. Long now have I been torn, seeking worthy approaches and the beginnings of your praises, O boy rightly beloved. On this side the years that stand on the threshold of life, on this side beauty seizes me, on that an early modesty, and shame and an honesty riper than his tender years. O where now is the whiteness suffused with a rosy blood, and the starry orbs and eyes that shed light upon the sky, and the gathered modesty of a chastened brow, the freeborn hair and, in the middle, the lovely border of the locks? Where now the mouth eloquent with coaxing complaints and the kisses, fragrant with spring flowers entwined, and the tears mingled with laughter, and the voice that, speaking deep within, was mingled with Hyblaean honey? To you the serpent would lay down its hiss, and savage stepmothers would wish to serve. I add nothing to true goods—alas, the milky neck! the arms, the neck never without its master's weight! O where now the not-far-off hope of coming youth and the longed-for honour of the cheeks, and the beard much sworn for you? All into ashes the heavy hour bore down and the day of hate: to us is left the remembering. Who will soothe your breast with the loved talk that made you glad? Who will relieve your cares and the secrets of your mind? Who, when you are inflamed with fierce bile and swelling at the slaves, will calm you and turn you back from anger against yourself? Who will take away the feast begun at your lips and the wine tasted and throw all into confusion with sweet pilfering? Who will break off your morning slumbers with his murmuring, laid upon the bedding, and delay your going with close embraces, and call you back to kisses from the very doorpost? Who, meeting you as you enter, will leap again into your face and hands, and throw his short arms about your shoulders? The house is dumb, I confess, the dwelling desolate, and mould is on the chambers, and sad silence at the tables! What wonder, if your devoted foster-father honours you with so great a funeral? You were the rest and harbour of his old age, you lately his delight, lately the sweet cares of his heart. No whirl of a barbarian platform turned you about, nor were you an infant for sale, mingled with Egyptian wares, who spoke prepared witticisms and rehearsed words in wanton fashion—for you cost dear and came slowly. Here was your home, hence your birth, and to your master's house once dear were both your parents, free for your joys, that you might not complain of your stock; but, taken straight from the womb, exulting he raised you up, and as with your first clear voice you greeted the stars, your master in his heart vowed you to himself, and held you embraced in his bosom and thought he had begotten you. Be it lawful for me to have said it, by the sacred parents' leave— and you, I pray, Nature, suffer it, to whom it is given to set the first laws over souls throughout the world: not all things does the nearest blood, or the offspring sent down through the line of birth, bind together; often within, new and adopted pledges creep, more closely linked. To have begotten children is a necessity, to have chosen brings joy. So coaxing Chiron, half-beast, outdid Haemonian Peleus for tender Achilles, nor did aged Peleus accompany his son to the Trojan arms, but Phoenix clung to his famous nursling. Evander prayed for the far-off returns of triumphant Pallas, faithful Acoetes watched the battles. And when from afar the father lingered among the bright stars, wave-wandering Dictys groomed winged Perseus. Why should I tell of mothers conquered by foster-mothers' love? Why of you, after the ashes and the cheated funeral of your mother, Bacchus, creeping more safely on the breast of Ino? Now, secure of her father, Ilia reigned in the Tuscan waters; Romulus wearied Acca as she carried him. I have myself seen grafted branches, on alien stock, go higher than their own. And now your mind and heart had made you father to him, though not yet his ways or his beauty: yet you loved even now his half-joined voices and his murmuring, his raw wailing and an infant's weeping. He, like a too-bold flower that stands tall in soft meadows, about to breathe its last at the first south winds, so, tender and before his time, with proud face and step had outdone his equals and left his years far behind, whether, his limbs bent in the chained wrestlings, he stood: you would think him conceived of an Amyclaean mother, headlong Apollo would exchange Oebalus's son for him, Alcides would weigh him against Hylas; or whether, Greek in dress, he ran through the Attic discourse of eloquent Menander: Thalia, rejoicing, would praise the sound and, wanton, would break her lovely hair with a rosy crown; or whether he told of the Maeonian elder and the toils of Troy, or the wanderings of Ulysses slowly returning: the father himself felt it, the very masters were amazed. Surely Lachesis, with ill-omened hand, touched his cradle, and Envy, holding the boy embraced in her lap, cherished him: she to adorn his cheeks and grown-out hair, this one to show him arts and fix in him words, which now we lament. He had begun, rising, to match the labours of Hercules in years, but childhood was still near him; yet now his step was strong and his stature larger than his garb, and his clothes seemed to shrink upon the boy, when, what clothes for you, what ornaments did your gentle master hasten to provide! Not to bind your breast in short mantles, nor to crowd your shoulders, narrowing them with a cloak; no shapeless folds for him, but, choosing weaving ever suited to his years, now he veiled him in a crimson cloak, now in a fold imitating the grass, now in a sweetly reddening purple, now he rejoiced to set his fingers ablaze with living gems: no train of attendants, no gifts cease: the bordered toga alone was wanting to his modest grace. Such was the fortune of the house, when the hostile Fate lifted her sudden hands. Why, goddess, do you cruelly bare your fierce claws? Does his beauty not move you, nor his pitiable age? Not savage Procne against her husband could have plucked this one, nor would the fierce Colchian have hardened into cruel rages, nor, had he been born of Aeolian Creusa: grim Athamas would have bent his mad bow away from him; him, though hating the ashes of Hector and Troy, Ulysses, about to hurl him from the Phrygian towers, would have wept. The seventh day, and already his cold eyes grow numb, already infernal Juno holds his hair in her hand. He, though the Fates press on his fragile years, sees you with dying face, and with falling tongue murmurs: into you he breathes all the remnants now of his empty breast; he remembers you alone, hears you alone as you call, and moves his lips for you, leaves his words for you, and forbids your groans, and consoles you in your grief. Yet I am grateful, Fates, that no slow death, as he lay, ate away the boy's grace, and that he went down to the shades whole and undefiled in body by any harm, just as he was. Why should I speak of the obsequies and the gifts lavish on the flames, and the funeral blazing with sad luxury? That the sad pyre rose for you in a crimson mound, that the flowers of Cilicia, that the gifts of Indian grass, and the liquids of the Arabs and Egyptians and Palestinians washed the hair that was to burn? Lavish, he longs to bring all and to set ablaze his whole fortune, Melior, hating his wealth now made desolate: but the envious fire cannot take it, and there are too few flames for the narrow gifts. Horror holds my senses, such as I dreaded you, at the last funeral, and beside the pyre, Melior, once most calm of men! Were you that man, who seemed cheerful and courteous? Whence this savagery and barbarous horror of the hands, while now, flung on the ground, you turn from the hateful light, now, grim, you tear alike your clothes and breast and press the beloved face and lick the cold kisses? There were the father and mother of the boy who lay there, sad—but the astonished parents gazed at you. What wonder? The whole crowd wept the impious thing, and the leading columns that the Mulvian causeway carries on the Flaminian track, while the innocent infant is given to the sad flames, and earns by his beauty and his age a groan: such as, taken approved from the sea to the Isthmian harbours, Palaemon, shipwrecked, lay beneath his mother set over him; so too Opheltes, playing in the grass of snake-bearing Lerna, greedy fire drank when his scales were torn open. Lay aside your fears, and cease to dread the threats of Death: the warder Cerberus shall not bark at him with his triple mouth, no Sister with flames, no rising hydras shall terrify him; nay, the grim boatman of the greedy skiff himself shall draw the barren banks and scorched shores nearer, so that the boy may have no hard task in climbing aboard. What does the offspring of Cyllene announce to me, rejoicing, with his wand? Is there anything so glad in a time so cruel? The boy had known the image and the lofty face of noble Blaesus, while often at home he saw you binding new garlands and wiping the like wax with your breast; him, when, ranging the shores of the Lethean flood, among the Ausonian nobles and the line of Quirinus, he recognized, timidly at first he joins his steps, approaching in silence, and tugs at the topmost garment, then follows more closely; for he no more spurns the one who draws him on, and believes him of unknown stock among his descendants. Soon, when he felt that this was the favourite, the pledge of a rare friend, and the boy who was the solace of lost Blaesus, he lifts him from the ground and binds him to his great neck, and long himself, rejoicing, carries him by hand, and offers what gifts soft Elysium has, the barren branches and the dumb birds and the flowers pale with their blunted bloom. Nor does he forbid him to remember you, but coaxing mingles their hearts and shares the boy's love by turns. This is the end of the lost one. Why do you not now soothe your wounds and lift your head sunk in grief? All things you see are done with, or doomed to die: nights and days pass away and the stars, nor does its own frame profit the solid earth. For who shall weep the deaths of a people, the mortal kind, the passing of the perishable crowd? These wars, these the seas demand; these love destroys, these madness and savage desire, to say nothing of diseases; these the stiffening lips of Winter, those the deadly Dog-star with its pitiless fire, these the pale Autumn awaits with its rain-bringing gape. Whatever has its rising fears its end. We shall all go, we shall go: Aeacus shakes the urn for the measureless shades. But he whom we mourn—happy, he has escaped men and gods and doubtful chance and the slippery ways of blind life, exempt from the Fates: he did not pray, did not fear nor earn to die: we, the anxious commons, we, the wretched, for whom it is uncertain whence the last day comes, what end of life, from what stars the thunderbolt threatens, what cloud sounds our doom—are you moved at all by these? But be moved willingly. Come hither, sent out from the dark threshold, you to whom alone it is given to obtain all things, Glaucias—the ferryman keeps not back the innocent souls, nor that companion of the cruel beast—: you soothe his breast, you forbid his cheeks to run, and fill his blessed nights with sweet talk and living looks, and deny that you have perished. Both his desolate sister, if you can, and his wretched parents, go on to win to comfort.

Hercules of Surrentum, belonging to Pollius Felix Pollius renews for you, Tirynthian, the interrupted rites, and assigns the reasons for the year's delay: that you are worshipped now in a greater dome, and no longer hold, poor, a bare shore and a roof habitable by wandering sailors, but gleaming doorposts and gables propped up with Greek metals, as though, purified again by the torches of an honest fire, you were climbing the heavens from the Oetaean flame. Scarce is there faith for eyes and mind: are you that inglorious keeper of an open threshold and a small altar? Whence this new hall and unlooked-for splendour for rustic Alcides? There are fates of gods, there are fates of places! O swift devotion! Here, lately, one might see barren sands, a mountain's flank sprinkled by the sea, and rocks shaggy with thorns, and ground that would suffer no footsteps. What fortune suddenly enriched the stiff crags? Did these walls come at a Tyrian quill or a Getic lyre? The year itself is amazed at the labours, and the cramped months, in their twelvefold bound, marvel at the long-lived work. A god brought the citadels and reared up his own, and the resisting rocks he removed, straining, and with his great breast pushed back the mountain: you would believe he had bidden his cruel stepmother. So come, whether, now free of the laws, you dwell in your father's Argos and tread upon Eurystheus sunk in his tomb, or whether you hold the throne of your own Jove and the stars won by your valour, and Hebe, girded, holds out to you a draught of blessed nectar, better than the rejected Phrygian: come hither and bring your genius to the rising temple. Not harmful Lerna, nor the fields of poor Molorchus, nor the dreaded field of Nemea and the Thracian caves demand you, nor the polluted altars of the Egyptian king, but a happy and simple house, ignorant of evil frauds, and a seat most worthy of heavenly guests. Lay aside your savage bows and the cruel troop of your quiver and the club drenched with the blood of many kings, and let go from your great shoulders the foe spread upon them: here for you a lofty couch is woven with Sidonian acanthus, and the bed grows rough with ivory figures. Come appeased and gentle, not turbulent with anger nor fearing servitude, but such as Maenalian Auge detained you, spent with revels and dripping with much wine, and such as Thespius, your father-in-law so many times over, beheld in amazement after the crimes of a wandering night. Here for you a festive wrestling-school, and the innocent rages of youths without the gauntlet, hold their yearly contests in a swift cycle. Here a priest is inscribed in the temple, his grandfather rejoicing, small as yet and like to you, when with your first hand you crushed the stepmother's monsters and grieved them slain. But what were the beginnings of the sudden temple, venerable one, tell me, come, Calliope; Alcides as your ally will sound the great strain, and his measures will be changed for the strung bow. It was the time when the most scorching axis of heaven leans upon the lands, and Sirius, struck by much Hyperion, keen, sets the panting fields ablaze, and now the day was at hand on which, fit for fugitive kings, the Arician grove of Trivia smokes, and with much torchlight the lake that knows of Hippolytus shines; Diana herself crowns her deserving dogs and wipes her darts and lets the beasts go safe, and the whole Italian land, its hearths chaste, keeps the Ides of Hecate holy. But I, although beneath the hills of Dardanian Alba I had my own estate, and the water running by the gift of the great leader sufficed at home to soothe my cares and ease the heats, was guesting at the rocks known by the Sirens' name and the home of eloquent Pollius, no stranger, ever learning the man's ways and his peace and the new flowers of the Muses and his untouched songs. By chance, while we kept Trivia's day on the wet shore and, heavy, shunned the narrow doors and accustomed roofs and warded off the sun with leaves and a spreading tree, the sky hid itself, and the bright light gave way to sudden clouds, and the west wind, thinned, with a heavier south wind grew wet; such a cloud as Saturn's daughter brought to Libya, while rich Elissa was given to her Ilian husband, and the nymphs, as witnesses, howled through the wilds. We scattered, and the slaves snatch away the festive feasts and the garlanded wines: nor was there anywhere for the banquet to move, although countless houses settled above the rejoicing fields and the mountain shone rich with many a roof: but the threatening clouds urged us to seek the nearest place, and the faith of fair weather, hurt, that would return. There stood a slender hut, called by the name of a sacred temple, and a small home pressed great Alcides in a humble dwelling, scarce able to cover the wave-wandering sailors and the searchers of the deep. Hither all our crowd we gathered, hither the feast and the rich couches and the throng of servants are packed, and the most welcome band of bright Polla. The doors did not hold us, and the narrow shrine fell short. The god blushed and laughed, and entered the beloved heart of Pollius, and embraced the man with coaxing arms. 'Are you,' he said, 'that bestower of wealth, who with lavish mind filled at once the houses of Dicarchus and youthful Parthenope? Who fixed for my mountain so many gables, so many green groves, so many rocks imitating faces, and bronzes, so many waxes living with painted light? For what was this house, what this land, before it could rejoice in you? Along a long track you covered the bare crags, and where there was only a footpath, now a high portico stands for you with set-out columns, that the way might not be mean. The shores of the curving coast you shut, with twin domes enclosing the warm nymphs. Scarce could I count your works; to me alone is Pollius poor and needy: yet glad I enter such a home, and the shore that you spread out I love. But the next seat looks down on this, and Juno secretly laughs at my threshold. Give me a temple and altars worthy of your endeavours, which ships would not wish to pass even with favouring sails, whither the ethereal father and the summoned throng of gods at the feast may come, and from a lofty temple his hostess-sister. Nor let it terrify you that the solid boss of the grudging mountain stands stiff against you and is never worn away by measureless age: I myself will be present and aid such great endeavours and break through the rough entrails of the unwilling earth. Begin, and, trusting in Hercules' urgings, dare. Not more swiftly stood the Amphionian citadels or the Pergamean labour.' He spoke and left his mind behind. And no delay: when the weapon is shaped by the written design, countless hands came together: theirs the care to cut the woods and lift the beams, theirs to sink the foundations in the soil. Part of the damp earth is baked, to protect against winters and shut out frosts, and the untamed flint melts in the curving furnace. But the chief labour is to hew away with the hand the opposing cliffs and the rocks that refuse the iron. Here the father of the place himself, the Tirynthian, his arms laid aside, sweats, and with strong axe the deformed ground, when the heavy sky is overspread with the shade of night, he himself digs, and the rich Goat-rocks and green Taurubulae echo back, and a huge echo of the sea returns to the lands. Not so loud does Aetna sound with its moving anvils, when Brontes and Steropes strike, nor is the crash greater from the Lemnian caves, when fiery Mulciber lets fall the aegis and adorns Pallas with chaste gifts. The crags shrink, and, returned under the rosy light, the craftsmen marvel at the work. Scarce does a second year pant out, and the rich Tirynthian from his huge citadel looks down on the waves and challenges the roof of his joined stepmother, and invites Pallas to worthy temples. Now the peaceful trumpets give their signals, now the sand, burning, smokes for the brave rites: these honours neither the Pisaean Jove nor the father of shady Cirrha would disdain. Nothing is sad in these places; let lamentable Isthmos give way, let grim Nemea give way: here a happier child offers sacrifice. The green Nereids themselves spring out of their own accord from their pumice caves: they cling to the wet crags and are not ashamed to watch in secret the naked wrestling-schools. And Gaurus watches, wooded with Icarian vine, and the grove that crowns Nesis fixed in the sea, and calm Limon and Euploea, an omen for ships, and Lucrine Venus, and from the Phrygian summit you, Misenum, shall learn the Greek trumpets, and kindly Parthenope laughs at the native rite and the naked contests of men and the small images of her own crown. Come too and yourself, glad, deign with unconquered hand the deeds of your own contest; whether to cleave the clouds with the discus, or to outstrip the swift west winds with the javelin, or whether it is sweet to you to knot the Libyan wrestling-bouts by hand, indulge the rites, and, if you have apples to spare from the Hesperides, set them in the venerable lap of Polla; for she can hold, and will not so far degrade the honour. But if she could take back her sweet glory and her green years, —give me pardon, Alcides—you might perhaps have spun for her your thread. These things I, glad and revelling at the rising altars, brought as my offerings. Now on the very threshold—I see him loosing his voice and uttering such words: 'A blessing on your spirit and your wealth, you who imitate my labours, who tame the stiff cliffs and the shameful wastes of barren nature, and turn to use the lairs haunted by wild beasts, and bring forth foully hidden powers; what rewards for your deserts shall I now pay you? What thanks shall I render? I will hold the threads of the Fates and draw out the distaffs—I know how to conquer hard Death—, I will turn away your mourning and forbid sad losses, and you, unharmed, I will renew with green old age, and grant you long to behold your young grandsons, until both this one is ripe for a bride and that one for a husband, and again from them a new brood and a forward band now creep over their grandsire's shoulders, now in a coaxing throng race vying to the kisses of calm Polla. For to my temples a bound of years shall never be set, while the engine of the flaming sky carries me, nor shall there be more dear to me Nemea and ancient Argos nor the Tiburtine house and the chambers of the sun, Gades.' So he speaks; and touching the fire rising on the altars and shaking his temples white with poplar foliage, he swore by the Styx and the thunderbolts of the ethereal father.
The Seventeenth Consulship of the Emperor Augustus Germanicus The purple comes, glad, to twice eight achievements,
and Germanicus opens a year made glorious by Caesar,
and rises with the new sun, among the great stars
shining more brightly himself, greater than the first dawn.
Let the Latian laws exult, rejoice, you curule chairs,
and let Rome, the prouder for it, beat the upper air
with her sevenfold ridge. More than all other heights
Evander's hill rejoices: the new fasces have entered the Palatine,
and the rest brought by a twelfth honour, the prayers granted,
the senate-house is glad to have conquered Caesar's modesty.
Janus himself too, the greatest restorer of measureless time,
lifts his face and from each threshold gives thanks,
he whom you bade, bound with Peace beside him,
compose all wars and swear allegiance to the laws
of the new Forum; behold, he raises his upturned hands
on this side and on that, and with his twin mouth speaks:
'Hail, great parent of the world, who prepare with me
to renew the ages: such your Rome desires always
to behold you in my month; thus it is fitting that the seasons
be born, the years begin; grant to the calendar joys
unbroken; let your shoulders be wrapped in folds of much purple
and the bordered robe sped from the hands of your own Minerva.
Do you see how a new splendour fills the temples, a higher fire
burns on the altars, and the very stars of my winter grow warm for you?
In your character too the squadrons and the tribes rejoice,
and the purple-clad fathers, and every honour
draws its light from the consul? What such, I pray, had the year before?
Come, tell me, mighty Rome, and with me, long Antiquity,
count over the calendars; recall no trivial precedents,
but only those that my Caesar would deign to surpass.
Augustus bore the fasces thirteen times in the gliding years,
but he began to earn them late; you in your youth
have outstripped your forebears. And how much you refuse,
how much you forbid! Yet you will yield to the prayers of the senate
and often promise this day. Beyond this a longer
order awaits, and happy Rome will give you as many curule chairs
three and four times over; with me you will found another age,
and the altar of your aged parent will be renewed for you;
a thousand trophies you will win—only grant triumphs:
Bactra remains to be bridled with new tributes, Babylon remains;
not yet is the Indian laurel in the lap of Jove,
not yet do the Arabs and the Seres sue for terms, not yet has every
year its honour, and the ten months long for your name.'
So Janus spoke, and gladly withdrew within his closed gate;
then all the gods stood open and gave from the glad
sky their signs; and a long youth to you, great leader,
Jupiter granted, and promised you his own years.
A Funeral Lament for Priscilla If I had a hand skilled to mould wax into likenesses,
or to give life to ivory or gold with stamped figures,
from these, Priscilla, I would frame a welcome solace
for your husband; for by his rare devotion he deserves
that, your face marked with Apelles's colour
or born from the hand of Phidias, you should be restored to his grief.
So he strives to snatch your shade from the pyre, and wages
a vast contest with Death, and wearies the cares
of craftsmen, and seeks in every metal to love you.
But mortal is the honour that the nimble hand labours.
We, rarest wife of a praised young man,
attempt to give you with our enduring lyre
just rites, long-lived and not to suffer an obscure end. Only let kindly Apollo
and Caesar, who comes to me ever with Apollo joined,
give assent: no better tomb to build than this.
Late indeed is the medicine prepared for so great a grief,
when the second winged wheel of Phoebus turns the year;
but while the wound was fresh and the house still black
in the first hurt, what access was there then to the wretched ear
of the bereaved husband? Then to weep and rend the garments
and weary the flocks of slaves and outdo all wailing
and beat at the Fates and the unjust gods above
with raging complaints was the only solace. Though Orpheus himself,
attended by woods and rivers, were present to soothe
the lamentations, and all his aunts to attend the bard,
all the priesthood of Apollo and Bacchus to cover him:
no songs, no strings could avail to soften the gods
of pale Avernus, or the Furies, when their hair had heard the sound:
so great a grief reigned in the thunderstruck breast!
Now even to lamentation the scar, now smooth, flees back
while we sing, and the rain of a husband's tears
presses heavy on his eyes. Have these eyes still pious weeping?
A wonder hard to believe! Sooner is the mother of Sipylus said
to have drained her cheeks, sooner the mournful dews
of Tithonis fail, or the sated mother of Achilles weary
of dashing storms against his tomb.
Blessing on your spirit! That the god marks, who turns the reins
of the world and, nearer than Jove, orders human deeds,
and sees you mourning: behold the secrets of his chosen minister!
From this too he takes proofs, that you love a shade
and tend a funeral. This is the chastest ardour,
this love that deserves to be approved by its lord, the censor.
No wonder, if Concord with a long, unbroken chain
joined you, mingled with breast laid to breast,
though she indeed had endured marriage before and the torches
with another husband, yet she cherished you, embraced with all
her heart and soul, as if joined to you in virginity;
just as the elm loves the vine wedded to its coeval
branch, and mingles the grove, and prays for a rich
autumn, and rejoices crowned with the dear clusters.
They are praised for their forebears, or for the gift of fair form,
who have lacked the goods of character, and, powerful by a false
praise, lack the true: though both your lineage shone
and your fair beauty was much to be desired by husbands,
from you came a greater honour, to have known one bed,
to have stirred one fire beneath your secret bones,
a love that neither the Phrygian ravisher could have corrupted,
nor the suitors of Dulichium, nor he, the fraternal adulterer,
who polluted a chaste marriage with Mycenaean gold.
If you offered the wealth of Babylon, if the weight of Lydia's treasure
and the powerful riches of the Indians and the Seres and the Arabs,
she would rather, in chaste poverty undefiled,
die, and pay her life for fame.
Nor was her brow grimly stern, nor too great the harshness in her manners,
but simple and cheerful faith, and grace mingled
with modesty; and if doubtful danger had called to greater things,
she would gladly, for her husband, have met the armed
bands and the lightning fires and the perils of the midmost sea,
the better that adverse fortune did not prove
what was your care for the marriage-bed. How great her pallor for her husband!
But by a better way your prayers earned the gods
kindly for your husband. While night and day you wearied
the powers, while you fell suppliant at every altar
and adored the gentle genius of your present lord.
You were heard; and Fortune came with kindly step.
For she saw the diligent quiet of the pious young man,
his unbroken faith and his breast girt with cares,
his watchful senses and his sober heart, worthy
to unfold such great affairs. She saw it—he who knows all
his servants' matters, and surrounds every side with chosen ministers.
No wonder: he sees risings and settings, what the south wind,
what the wintry north wind does; and the counsels of the sword and the toga
he approves, and the very mind. Upon those shoulders, subdued,
he laid an immense burden and a weight scarce to be handled
—for no other care in the sacred house is more manifold—:
to send forth far into the wide world
the orders of the Romulean leader, and to handle with his hand
the strength and the measures of empire; what laurels come from the north,
what the wandering Euphrates, what the bank of the double-named Hister,
what the standards of the Rhine may bear; how far the farthest world
has yielded, and Thule, surrounded by its retreating, resounding flood—
for all the javelins lift glad foliage,
and no lance is marked with a fatal feather—
besides, if the lord distributes his trusty swords,
who is fit to bridle the maniples in their hundreds,
who should be sent among them as a knight, who to command a cohort,
whom a higher rank of bright tribune befits,
who is worthier to give the signal to a bridle-bearing squadron;
to foreknow also a thousand changes, whether the Nile
has drowned the fields, whether Libya has sweated with the rain-bringing south wind;
and were I to count all, no more does the winged Tegean herald
announce with his interpreting wand from the lofty stars,
nor the Junonian maiden who falls through the liquid air
and binds the rain in her painted arc,
nor she who, with winged course, carries your laurels, Germanicus,
Fame, outrunning the day and leaving the slow Arcadian
beneath the stars and the daughter of Thaumas in mid-heaven.
How the gods, Priscilla, and men beheld you on that
kindly day, when first your husband was set near such great
affairs! You almost outdid the joys
of the man himself, while with poured-out heart, prostrate before
the sacred feet of a lord so greatly deserving, you rolled
so great things. Not so on the Aonian summit does he rejoice
whom the Delian father set over the chasms of the secret cave,
nor he to whom Bacchus gave the venerable right of the first thyrsus
and the standards of the thunderstruck band.
Nor for this was her quiet or her goodness changed, nor did she swell
with prosperity: the same tenor of mind and modest manners
remain as her fortune grows; anxious, she nurses the cares
of her husband and at once urges and softens his labours.
She herself hands out the modest fare and sober cups,
and counsels to follow the lord's example; like the Apulian wife
of a thrifty farmer, or the Sabine woman scorched by the sun,
who sees, when the stars now look forth, that the time
of her wearied man is at hand, and quickly the tables and the couches
she sets, and waits for the sound of the returning plough.
I speak of little things: she would go with you, a companion through the icy north
and the Sarmatian winters and the Hister and the pale frosts
of the Rhine, with you, her spirit hardened through all the heats;
and, if the camp allowed, she would wish to bear the quiver,
would wish to guard her side with the Amazon's shield,
while she might see you in the dusty cloud of wars
near the thunderbolt of Caesar's horse, brandishing the divine
weapons and sprinkled with the sweat of the great spear.
Thus far the kindly lyre. Now is the time to lay aside your leaves,
Phoebus, and to doom your locks to the mournful cypress.
What god bound Fortune and Envy together
in a kinship never at peace? Who bade the unjust
goddesses war for ever? Will she mark no house
that this one does not at once eye with a grim glance
and overturn its joys with cruel hand?
The household flourished, glad and unshaken:
nothing sorrowful—for what, however faithless and fickle,
could be feared from Fortune, with Caesar so favourable?
The envious Fates found a way, and savage force
entered the pious home; so the vineyards are blasted
with the malignant south wind; so the tall harvest grows old
with too much rain; so the breeze, meeting the swift ship,
grudges it, and clouds over the favourable sails;
Priscilla's surpassing beauty is plucked by Fate;
as the tall pine, the leafy glory of the forests,
whether by Jove's evil fire or now loosed at the root,
fails and, despoiled, murmurs back to no breeze,
what avail goodness or chaste faith, what the honoured
powers of the gods? On every side the dark nets of death
hedged the wretched woman about; the sisters' hard threads
are stretched, and only the last part of the spun thread remains.
No throng of slaves, no laborious art of the healers
availed her ills; yet her companions everywhere with feigned
face counterfeit hope; she marks her weeping husband,
he now in vain begs the streams of infernal Lethe
undrunk, now anxious at every altar
weeps and seals the doors and with his breast wipes
the thresholds; now he calls the entreatable power of great
Caesar—alas, the harsh course of fate! Is there anything
he may not do? How great a delay could have been added
to mortal years, if you, father, held all
control! Mocked Death would groan in her blind pit
longer, and the empty Parcae would have laid by their threads.
And now her face falls, and over her eyes the last
wandering, and her ears grow dull, save when the husband's voice alone
is known; him alone, returned from the midst of death,
her mind beholds, him she clasps bravely with feeble arms,
her unmoving eyes turned toward him; not on the last sun
does she choose to sate her sight, but on her sweet husband.
Then dying she thus consoles her like-souled lover:
'Part of my soul that shall live on, to whom would that I could
leave the years that hard Atropos snatches from me:
spare, I pray, your tears; do not strike your breast
with cruel wailing, nor torment your wife's fleeing shade.
I leave the marriage-chamber indeed, yet with the order of death unbroken,
since I go first: I have lived out times better than long old age;
I saw you long ago shining in every flower,
I saw you draw nearer and nearer to the lofty right hand;
now over you the Fates have no power, nor any longer the gods above:
these things I carry with me. Do you press on gladly
on your begun path; love untiringly the sacred side
and the mighty genius; now, what you yourself desire to be bidden,
give to the Capitoline seat eternal gold,
that the sacred face of Caesar may shine with its hundredfold weight
and mark the love of his own worshipper;
so I shall see neither the Furies nor the worse
Tartarus, and shall be admitted happy to the Elysian shores.'
This she says, sinking, and embraces his joined limbs,
and not sad, transferred her clinging soul to her husband's lips,
and with her dear right hand pressed down her own eyes.
But the young man, his breast set aflame with great grief,
now fills the widowed home with savage cry,
now longs to loose the sword, now stretches to the high
places—his companions scarce hold him back—; now with mouth sealed
he lies on the lost one, and savage drives the sunken grief
deep in his heart; as the Odrysian bard, sluggish
at the sight of his wife, his quill laid down by the Strymon,
was stunned, and wept the sad pyre without a song,
he too would have broken off the spans of his upright life,
that you might not go uncompanioned to Tartarean chaos,
but the faithful mind of his leader forbids it, and the awe
of the sacred command and a greater love. Who with worthy song
could read through the funeral rites and the deadly gifts of the sad procession?
There all heaped in a long swarm
flows the spring of the Arabs and the Cilicians, and the flowers of Saba
and the harvest of the Indians soon to burn, and incense snatched
from Palestinian temples, with the Hebrew liquors
and the Corycian foliage and the Cinyrean buds; and on a high
couch she herself reclines, shaded with Seric
and Tyrian covering, but in all the procession the husband alone
is gazed upon; on him the eyes of great Rome are turned
as on one bearing young sons to their last pyres:
such grief is in his face, so much of night
his hair and cheeks have; her, loosed in a tranquil end
and happy, they call; for the husband they shed their tears.
There is a place before the city, where huge Appia
first arises, and where, by the Italian Almo, Cybele
lays down her grief and no longer remembers the Idaean streams;
here, veiled softly in Sidonian purple,
her peerless husband—for he could not endure the smoking pyres
and the cry of the funeral fire—laid you, Priscilla, on a blessed
couch. Nothing can the longer years
pluck away, nothing can the toils of time spoil,
once your limbs were dried: such wealth the venerable marble
breathes. Soon, changed into various
shapes, you are made new: in this bronze Ceres, in this bright Cnossian,
in that dome Maia, in this stone Venus, and not unchaste.
The powers, not disdaining, receive your comely
features; the slaves stand round and the throng accustomed
to your service; then duly couches and tables are prepared,
unfailing. This is a house, a house! Who would call it a sad
sepulchre? With the husband's devotion thus rightly seen
you would at once cry out: 'Here is, I recognize, the minister
of him who lately founded the shrine of an eternal race
and set his stars in another heaven.'
So, when a great ship from the Pharian shore
looses its new course, and now on either side the countless cables
and the broad arms of the sail-bearing mast it stretches forth
and has entered upon its ways, a narrow skiff goes by the same
sea, and claims for itself a part of the immense south wind.
Why now, choicest of young men, do you nurse immoderate weeping
in your heart, and long forbid your grief to depart?
Surely you do not fear that Priscilla may tremble at the Cerberean
barkings? He is silent to the pious! That a too-slow boatman
may delay and drive her from the shallows? He carries the deserving
at once, and gently sets the shades in his welcoming skiff.
Besides, if ever a shade praised by a pious husband
comes, Proserpina bids the glad torches go
and the old heroines, come forth from the sacred caves,
with purple light loosen the sad darkness,
and strew garlands and Elysian flowers before the soul;
so Priscilla enters the shades; there with suppliant hand
she begs the Fates for you, appeases the kings of grim Avernus
for you, that, the bounds of human life fulfilled,
you may leave the lands and a lord that calls you their healer, and yourself
leave the earth, a young man grown old! The sure sisters swear to her prayer.

Epithalamium for Stella and Violentilla Whence have the hills of Latium rung with sacred song? For whom, Paean, do you stir new quills, and from your flowing shoulder hang the eloquent ivory? See, far off the goddesses come down from tuneful Helicon and shake the ninefold torch, the solemn flame for a wedding's union, and the singing water from Pierian springs— among whom, her face full of wantonness, Elegy draws near, taller than her custom, and urges and courts the goddesses, ready to prop her alternate foot, and longs to be seen a tenth among them, and slips in mingled, undetected, among the sisters. The mother of Aeneas's line led the bride by the hand herself, her eyes cast down and blushing with sweet modesty; she herself prepares the couch and the rites, and, in a Latin girdle disguising the goddess, tempers her hair and face and cheeks and, made less, delights to walk as a new bride. I know the day, and the reasons for the rite: it is you that chorus sings—throw wide the doors!—you, Stella; for you Phoebus and Euhan and the winged Tegean from his Maenalian shade bring garlands; nor does coaxing Love nor the Grace cease to scatter your longed-for wife's snowy limbs in embrace with countless flowers and a fragrant shower. You now catch roses upon your brow, now lilies mixed with violets, and screen them from your mistress's snowy face. So the day was at hand, ordained by the Fates in white wool, on which the marriage of Stella and Violentilla, proclaimed, should be cried aloud—let cares and fears give way, let the lying tricks of slanting verse cease, Rumour, be silent: that love, once loosed, has come beneath the law and bitten the curb; the gossip of the crowd is spent, and the citizens have seen the kisses long talked of. Yet you, astonished, though such a night's plenty is granted you, still wish, and dread your vows now allowed by a favouring power; lay down, sweet poet, your sighing, lay it down: she is yours. You may go through the open threshold, freely set ajar, come and go: now nowhere is there doorkeeper or law or shame; sate yourself at last in the embrace you sought— it is yours!—and remember together the hard nights. A worthy reward indeed, even if Juno had given you the labours of Hercules, even if the Fates had granted you to face Stygian monsters, even were you swept through the Cyanean surge. For her sake it would have been worth running, trembling, the Pisaean course and hearing the roar of Oenomaus in pursuit; nor, had you sat, a reckless shepherd on Dardanian Ide; these would have been gifts—nor though gracious Tithonia caught you up instead and bore you away through the air in her chariot. But what cause brought the marriage-bed and unhoped joys to the poet? Here, while the doorposts seethe with the throng and the halls, and many a threshold is struck by many a wand, here, charming Erato, teach me. There is leisure to start fitting talk, and the learned household knows how to listen. By chance, where the Milky Way stands in the calmed sky, nurturing Venus was lying, lately driven from her chamber by night, loosed from her Getic husband's hard embrace. A tender troop of Loves presses about the goddess's bolster and couch; they ask for signals: where to carry their torches, what hearts she bids them pierce; whether she would rather rage on land or in the waves, whether to set the gods at odds, or vex the Thunderer still further. Her own mind not yet fixed, no will settled in her heart, she lies weary on the bedding, where once the Lemnian chains, witnesses of her fault, crept over the bed when it was caught. Then a boy out of the winged crowd—he in whom is most fire, in face and in the light hand whose arrow never failed— from the midst of the band thus sweetly speaks in his tender voice; his quivered brothers held their silence. 'You know, mother,' he says, 'that no hand of mine is sluggish in its service; whomever of men or gods you have appointed, he burns; yet sometimes by tears and a suppliant hand and by prayers and entreaties grant that a man be moved, O mother: for we are not made of hard adamant, but are your own kindred. There is a young man, famous, of Latin stock, whom, sprung from patrician forebears, nobility rejoiced to bear, and at once, foreseeing his beauty, gave him a surname from our heaven. Him I once, with my whole quiver—a sweetness to you— mischievously and with thick shaft pierced as he trembled. Though much sought by Ausonian mothers as a son-in-law, I subdued him, conquered, and bade him bear the yoke of a powerful mistress and to hope through long years; but her I touched only lightly with the topmost torch—for so you bade—sparing, and with an idle bow. From that time how great the fires that anxious young man endures, I am witness, astonished; how through night and day he bears me pressing on him: never on any one have I leaned more fiercely, mother, nor dug the wounds again and again so deep. I have seen Hippomenes too eager to run the cruel field, and not so pale was he even at the goal itself; I have seen the arms of the youth of Abydos vying with the oars and praised his hands, and often, as he swam, I lit his way before him: less was the heat that warmed those savage waters. You, young man, having passed beyond your former loves— I myself marvelled that you held out through such fevers and strengthened your spirit and dried with coaxing feathers your eyes wet with weeping. How often Apollo complained to me that his poet grieved so! Now, mother, grant the marriage he loves; he is our comrade and devoted standard-bearer: he could have told of arms-bearing labours and the famous deeds of heroes and fields streaming with blood, but you gave him the quill, and he chose rather to walk a gentle poet, and to weave laurel into our myrtle. He recounts the falls of youths and their wounds, his own and others'— ah, how great, mother, is his reverence for the Paphian power: it was he who wept the fate of our dove.' He had finished; he hung upon his mother's tender neck, coaxing, and warmed her breast with feathers laid against it; she replies, her face not scorning to be asked: 'A great thing indeed and rare for men, those whom I have approved. A Pierian youth desires the boon: this woman, whose surpassing ornament of beauty I admired—where the glory of her fathers and the honour of her line contended—as she fell to earth I caught her up and cherished her in my bosom, nor did my hand cease, my son, to smooth her neck and cheeks and to draw rich balsam through her hair: to me a sweet image sprang forth. From afar behold the honours of her lofty brow and her piled-up hair. Measure how far she stands out beyond Latin matrons: as much as the Latonian maid overtops the nymphs, and as much as I myself stand above the Nereids. She was worthy to rise with me from the dark-blue waves and to take her seat upon my shell; and if she could have climbed to the flaming dwellings and entered these halls, you Loves yourselves would have strayed. Though I lavished blessed wealth on her, she surpasses her riches in spirit; now I complain that the greedy Chinese strip too narrow a grove, and that the seeds of Clymene fail, nor do the green sisters weep enough, and that too few fleeces now redden with Sidonian dye, and that the crystal of long-lived snows is too rarely chilled. For her I have bidden Hermus and Tagus run down with golden silt, and—not enough for her adornment—bidden Glaucus and Proteus and every Nereid seek Indian necklaces. Had you seen her, Phoebus, through the Thessalian fields, Daphne would wander unafraid; had she been seen on Naxos's shore beside the bed of Theseus, Euhan in flight would have left the Cnossian girl deserted. But had not Juno appeased me with long complaints, the ruler of heaven would have taken false wings and horns for her, and into this woman truly would Jupiter have fallen in the gold. Yet she shall be given to the young man for whom you, my chief power, my son, long—though, grieving, she often denies she will bear the yoke of a second marriage. I have felt that she herself now gives way and has in turn grown warm toward the man.' So speaking she lifted her starry limbs, and passing out from her chamber's proud threshold she called the Amyclaean swans to the reins. Love yokes them, and bearing his glad mother through the clouds sits on the doubled pole; now the towers of Ilian Tiber: the lofty house throws open its bright dwellings, and the joyful swans clapped the gleaming thresholds. A seat worthy of a goddess, that does not look mean beside the shining stars. Here is Libyan and Phrygian marble, here the hard rock of Laconia greens; here is veined onyx, and a vein matching the deep sea, and shining cliffs; here purple often envies the Oebalian and the master of the Tyrian cauldron. The roofs hang propped on countless columns, the beams gleam, soaked with Dalmatian ore. A cool shade let down from ancient woods shuts out the rays, and clear fountains live in the marble. Nor does nature keep its turns: here Sirius is cold, winter is warm, and the house tempers the changed year to itself. Nurturing Venus exults at the sight, and at the dwelling of her powerful foster-child, no less than if she were entering Paphos from the deep sea, the Idalian halls, and the temples of Eryx. Then she addressed the woman herself, reclining on her solitary couch: 'How long this drowsiness, this propriety of an empty bed, O you, dear to me among the Laurentine girls? What measure is there of virtue and good faith? Will you never bow your neck to a husband's yoke? A sadder age will come. Use your beauty, enjoy gifts that are fleeting: not for this did I give you such grace and a proud face and myself, that you should pass through your years widowed as though you were not dear to me. Enough and more than enough to have scorned your former suitors; for here is one given to you with his whole heart, who, among all, admires and loves you alone, needing neither beauty nor lineage; for what young men through the city, what girls, have not learned his cultured songs? Him too—so may the indulgence of the Ausonian ruler continue—you shall see lift up the twelvefold rods before his time; surely even now he has moved the Cybelian threshold and read the Euboean Sibyl's verse, and now the Latin father, whose mind it is my right to know beforehand, will grant the young man purple robes and the curule ivory, and—this the greater glory— the Dacian spoils and fresh laurels to celebrate. So come, join in marriage and take leisure from his youth. What nations, what hearts have I not yoked with my torch? The flocks of birds and beasts and of the hard wild creatures have not refused me; the very air I loose into wedlock with the earth when the clouds grow thin with rain; so the chain of things and the world's age renews itself. Whence the new glory of Troy and the snatcher of the burning gods, had I not been joined to a Phrygian husband? Whence would Lydian Tiber have repeated my Iuli? Who would have set the walls of sevenfold Rome, the Latian head of empire, had not a Dardanian priestess seized Mars by stealth—and not against my will?' With these words she soothes her and breathes into her silence the honour of marriage; back to her mind come now the gifts and prayers and tears, and the man's complaints, watchful near the threshold, and Asteris, sung by the poet through the whole city, Asteris before the feast, Asteris by night, Asteris at dawn, more than Hylas ever was cried aloud; and now she begins, gladly, to bend her stubborn heart and now to seem harsh to herself. A blessing on your couch, gentlest of Latian poets, that, having measured out the hard road and the toils begun, you have reached your haven; just as the runaway stream of bright Pisa, inflamed from afar with love of a foreign water, draws its untainted flood through a sunken channel, until, brought forth at last, it drinks with panting mouth the Sicilian springs; the Naiad marvels at the sweet kisses and cannot believe her husband has come through the sea. What a day was then yours, Stella, in the gods' bright gift, with what longing did your heart leap up, when, propitious, your mistress's face nodded assent to the sweet marriage! You seemed to walk the sky and stray among the gleaming poles. Less did the shepherd exult on Amyclaean sands when Helen came to the Idaean ships; Thessalian Tempe saw no such Peleus, when Chiron from his high-reared horse looked out and saw Thetis approaching the Haemonian shores. How long the stars delay! How slow is the Dawn to the husband's vows! But far off, as soon as they sensed that Stella's wedding was being made ready, the Letoan father of poets and Semele's Euhan, the one stirs his bands at Ortygia, the other at swift Nysa. For the one the Lycian mountains and the cool shade of Thymbra and Parnassus resound; for the other Pangaea echoes back and Ismarus and the once festive shores of Naxos. Then they entered the dear doors, and for the tuneful comrade one brings the lyre, one the tawny fawnskin with its dappled back, one the thyrsus, one the quills; one binds his brows with the inspired laurel, another presses his hair with a Minoan crown. Scarce had the day come forth, and already the wedding omens were at hand, and now each house seethes with festive pomp. The doorposts green with leaves, the crossroads blaze with flames, and the most crowded quarter of measureless Rome rejoices. Every dignity, all the rods, come to the thresholds, every bordered robe is jostled in plebeian tumult: here the knights, here the stole jostles, mixed in the throng of youths. They call them both happy; but in the crowd the more envied the man. Already, leaning against the doorpost, Hymen seeks for the bridal chamber a song still untouched, with which to soothe the poet; Juno grants the venerable bonds, and Concord marks the rite with twin torch. This was that day: let the bridegroom himself sing the night! So far as one may know, just so, vanquished by deceiving sleep, did warlike Ilia lay her side upon the river-bank; not such did Lavinia dye her snowy face, when she blushes with Turnus looking on; not such did Claudia look back upon the people, a maiden, when the ship had moved. Now to work, companions of the Aonian maids and ministers of the tripod, to contend in your several measures: let the inspired band advance, crowned with fillets and ivy, as each is mighty with his triumphing lyre. But chiefly you who at the line's last step would cheat the noble work: give songs worthy of the festal couch. This day, with Cos applauding, Philetas himself and old Callimachus, and Propertius from his Umbrian grot, would have wished to praise; nor Ovid, sad in his own Tomis, nor Tibullus rich by his shining hearth. For me at least no single love, no simple cause of singing, draws me on: with you the Muses are alike and joined, Stella, for me, and as equals we revel together at the altars and drink the kindred water from learned streams; and you, at your birth, my own Parthenope first received in her lap, and on our soil, sweet glory, you crept as a child. Let the Euboean land rise up to the bright sky and Sebethus swell with pride in her lovely foster-child; nor let the Naiads of Lucrine in their sulphurous caves, nor the leisure of Pompeian Sarnus, please themselves more. Come now, hasten famous descendants for Latium, to rule the laws, to govern the camps, to play at songs. Let kindly Cynthia speed the tenth month to its birth, but spare her, Lucina, I pray: and you yourself, boy, spare your mother, do not hurt her tender womb, do not the breasts that stand there; and when nature, in her silent retreat, has formed your face, may you carry much of your father's beauty, more of your mother's. And you, fairest in form of Italian women, possessed at last by a deserving husband, cherish the bond long sought: so shall you suffer no loss of beauty; so, green with the flower of long youth, let your face endure, and let this beauty be slow to grow old.

The Surrentine Villa of Pollius Felix Among walls known by the name of the Sirens, and the rocks weighed down by the temple of Tyrrhenian Minerva, there stands a lofty villa, watcher of the Dicarchean deep, where the field is loved by Bromius, and over the high hills the vine is sun-scorched and does not envy the Falernian presses. Hither, after the five-yearly games of my native lustrum, when now a sluggish quiet sat upon the course and the white dust, the contest turned to the Ambracian wreaths, across the strait of my homeland the eloquence of calm Pollius and the youthful grace of bright Polla drew me, when I was already eager to bend my steps where, by the known track, the Appian Way, queen of long roads, is worn. But the delays were welcome; in a calm crescent the waters break through the curving cliffs on either side; nature gives place, and between the mountain there comes a single shore, and goes out into the land with overhanging crags. The first grace of the place: with twin domes the baths steam, and from the land a sweet nymph runs to meet the bitter sea. Here the light troop of Phorcus and Cymodoce with her dripping hair, and green Galatea, long to bathe. Before the house the dark-blue ruler of the swelling wave keeps watch, guardian of the harmless home: with his friendly brine the temples foam. Alcides guards the happy fields; the harbour rejoices under a twin power: this one keeps the lands, this one withstands the savage waves. Wondrous the calm of the sea: here the wearied waters lay aside their fury, and the mad south winds breathe more gently, here the headlong storm dares less, and with no tumult the modest pools lie, imitating their master's ways. Thence a portico creeps up over the slanting heights, a city's work, and tames the rough rock along its long ridge, where before were suns mingled with dark dust and the cheerless wildness of the way; now to go is a pleasure: just as, if you should climb the high summit of Bacchic Ephyre, a covered path leads from Ino's Lechaeum. No—not if Helicon should indulge me all its streams and Pimplea should outdo my thirst, and the hoof of the flying horse should grant abundance, and Phemonoe should unlock her chaste and secret fountains, or those which my Pollius, under Phoebus's auspices, troubled with his urn plunged deeper— could I be able to match in Pierian measures the countless forms and adornments of the places. Scarce in the long array did my eyes suffice; scarce, while I am led through each, did my steps suffice. What a throng of things! Should I marvel first at the genius of the place, or of its master? This house looks on the risings and the tender radiance of Phoebus; that one holds the setting sun and refuses to dismiss the spent light, when now the day is weary and the shadow of the dark mountain falls upon the waters, and the mansions float on the glassy sea. These roofs roar with the sea's clamour, these are ignorant of the sounding waves and prefer the silences of the land. On these places nature smiled; here, conquered, she yielded to the dresser and, teachable, grew tame to unknown uses. A mountain was here, where you see level ground; and lairs there were, where now you go beneath the roofs; where now you see lofty groves, here there was not even earth: the owner tamed it, and the soil, following him as he shaped the cliffs and stormed them, rejoices. Now behold the rocks learning the yoke, and the houses entering, and the mountain bidden to retreat. Now let the hand of the Methymnaean bard and his lyre yield to you, and the Theban harp, and the glory of the Getic quill: you too move rocks, and the deep groves follow you. Why should I tell of the old figures of wax and bronze, if Apelles's colours rejoice to have given them life, if Phidian hands, in still empty—yet admirable—Pisa, have carved anything, or what was bidden by Myron's art or by Polyclitus's chisel to live, and the bronzes, more precious than gold, from the Isthmian ashes, the faces of leaders and bards and of the wise men of old, whom you take care to follow, whom with your whole breast you feel, free of cares and, your mind composed in quiet virtue, ever your own? Why should I unroll the thousand summits and the changing scenes of viewing? Each has its own delight, and a sea proper to every chamber, and across the lying Nereus its own land serves the different windows: this one sees Inarime, thence rough Prochyta appears; here lies open the armour-bearer of great Hector, there Nesis, circled by the sea, breathes back its malign air; hence Euploea, a happy omen to wandering ships, and Megalia, jutting out, that strikes the curving waves, and Limon grieves, your Limon, with its master reclining across from it and gazing far off at the Surrentine mansions. Yet one chamber, one above all stands forth, far off, which sets before you Parthenope on a straight line of sea: here are the rocks chosen from deep within Greek quarries; what the vein of Eastern Syene sprinkles, what the Phrygian axes have dug from sad Synnas through the fields of mourning Cybele, where on the painted marble a white field is set off by a purple ring; here too what was cut from the Amyclaean mount of Lycurgus, that greens and imitates soft grasses on the rocks, here the yellow stones of the Numidians gleam, and Thasos and Chios, and Carystos that rejoices to watch the waves: all, turned toward them, salute the Chalcidian towers. A blessing on your spirit, that you approve what is Greek, that you frequent Greek fields: nor let the walls of Dicarchus that bore you envy! We shall the better possess our learned foster-son. Why should I now tell of the riches of the countryside and the new tillage thrown out into the sea, and the rocks wet with Bacchic nectar? Often through autumn, when Lyaeus is already ripening, a Nereid has climbed the crags and, hidden in the shade of night, wiped her eyes, dripping, with the ripe vine-shoot, and snatched the sweet grapes from the hills. Often too the vintage has been splashed by the neighbouring wave, and Satyrs have fallen in the shallows, and the mountain Pans have longed to catch naked Doris through the waters. Be happy, land, to both your masters, for years of the Mygdonian and Pylian elder, nor change your noble servitude, nor let the Tirynthian hall outdo you in culture, and the bay of Dicarchus, nor let the coaxing vineyards of Therapnaean Galaesus please these masters more often. Here, where Pollius plies the Pierian arts, whether he turns over the counsels the Gargettian author gives, or strikes our lyre, or weaves discordant songs, or, threatening, draws the avenging iambus: hence the light Siren flies from the crags to better songs, hence Tritonia listens with her crest astir. Then the swift winds lay themselves down, the very seas are forbidden to make their noise, the dolphins emerge from the deep and are drawn, coaxing, to the learned lyre, and stray among the rocks. Live, richer than the treasures of Midas and the Lydian gold, happy beyond Trojan and Euphratean diadems, whom no ambiguous rods, no fickle crowd, no laws, no camps shall carry away—you who with a great heart tame hope and fear, loftier than every vow, exempt from the Fates and refuting indignant Fortune; whom, in the doubtful whirlwind of affairs, the last day shall not surprise, but ready to depart and full of life. We, a base crowd, ready always to serve perishable goods and to wish for more, are scattered to chances: from the lofty citadel of your mind you look down on the wanderers and laugh at human joys. There was a time when the votes of two lands tore you apart and you were borne aloft through two cities, venerable here to the Dicarchean colonists, there adopted by mine, and lavish alike to these and those, hot with youth and proud of the wandering of the quill; but now, the mist of things dispersed, you behold the truth— while others in their turn are tossed on that deep— and your bark, unshaken, has entered the secure harbours and the calm rest. So go on, and never send your retired ship out into our storms. And you, far the most learned among Latin daughters-in-law, and equal to your husband in mind, whose heart no cares, no threats furrow your brow, but always bright joys and a pleasure in your face that knows nothing of cares; no unlucky chest strangles your hoarded riches, nor does the loss of greedy interest torment your mind: your wealth is set out, and there is a learned moderation in enjoying it. No hearts cohere under a better god, no other minds did Concord teach. Learn, secure, you whose mingled torches from your breast have come together for the long years, and a holy love keeps the laws of chaste friendship. Go through the years and ages, and outstrip the titles of ancient fame.

Propempticon for Maecius Celer Gods, whose love it is to keep the bold keels safe and to soothe the savage perils of the windy deep, spread the sea soft and turn to my vows a calm will, and let no gentle wave drown out the one who prays: 'A great and rare deposit, Neptune, we give to your deep, a young man is entrusted to the doubtful main, Maecius, and he prepares to carry across the seas the greater part of our soul. Bring forth your kindly stars and settle on the twin horns of the yard-arm, sons of Oebalus; for you let sea and sky shine: far off drive the stormy stars of your Ilian sister, I pray, and shut them from all the sky. You too, dark-blue band of the sea, Nereids, to whom honour and the fortune of the second realm has fallen —if it be lawful for me to name the great sea's stars—, rise from the glassy caves of foaming Doris, and the bays of Baiae and the shores teeming with warm waves vie in a calm swimming to circle round. Seeking where the high ship is, which the noble nursling of warlike Ausonia, Celer, rejoices to climb. Nor is it long to seek: but lately, beyond the seas, the first to land at the Dicarchean shores the heavy Egyptian year, the first to salute Capreae, and on the right margin sprinkled the Mareotic wines of Tyrrhenian Minerva. Gird each side of this ship in your soft circle, and, your tasks shared out, you stretch the hempen cables of the mast, you bind the topsails to the highest yards, you open the sails to the west winds; let part replace the benches, part lower into the waters the rudders of the curving stern; let there be those for whom the heavy lead-plummet explores the depths, and those who tie astern the boat that will follow and pluck up from deep within the hooked anchor-cables; let one temper the tides and bend the sea toward the dawn: let none of the grey-green sisters be free of her office; hence let Proteus, with much body, and Triton, with twin body, swim ahead, and Glaucus, who lost his loins to sudden monsters, as often as he glides to his fatherland's shores, striking shore-loving Anthedon with his coaxing tail. But you above all, Palaemon, with your divine mother, assent, if it is my love to lay open your Thebes, and I sing of Phoebean Amphion with no degenerate quill. And the father who breaks the winds in his Aeolian prison, to whom the varied blasts and every breath through the seas of the world and the storms and the rain-clouds obey, let him press Boreas and Eurus and Notus more closely, the mountain set against them: let the sky be free for Zephyr alone, let him alone drive the ships and skim above the highest waves, unceasing on the sea; until, with no whirlwind, he assigns your glad sails to the Paraetonian banks.' We are heard. He himself calls the ship and chides the lingering sailors. Lo, my heart already with timid cold slips down, and I cannot, though the horror of the omen warns me, close the tears suspended on the margin of my eyes. And now the sailor has parted the ship from land with the cable loosed and let down the narrow gangway into the sea. The savage master from the stern with a long shout scatters the embraces and tears apart the faithful kisses, nor is it allowed to linger long on the dear neck, yet I will go onto the land last of all the throng, nor depart until the ship is already withdrawing. Who made for wretched living creatures this rough and severed sea a path, and drove the pious nurslings of the solid earth out into the waves and sent them into the gaping deep, bold in his ingenuity? For no rasher was that valour which joined cold Pelion to the summit of Ossa and twice pressed panting Olympus beneath the ridges. Was it so little to cross the slow marshes and pools, and to set narrow rivers beneath bridges? We go into the sheer abyss, and from every side flee our native lands, shut in a scanty plank and a bare sky. Hence the fury of the winds and the indignant storms and the roaring of the sky and the more thunderbolts for the Thunderer. Before ships the seas were torpid in sluggish sleep, nor did Thetis dare to foam, nor the waves to scatter clouds: the waters swelled at the sight of the keels, and the storm rose against man. Then the Pleiades were cloudy, and the Olenian Goat; then Orion was worse than his wont. I complain justly: see, the ship, driven through the wandering waves, flees, little by little smaller, and far off conquers my keeping eyes, holding so many fears clasped in its slender wood. And you who above the rest, pledge of our love, will carry, Celer—with what heart shall I now bear my sleep or how endure my days? What messenger to one fearing everything, whether the smooth wave has let you pass the raging mouth of the Lucanian sea, whether twisted Charybdis heaves, or the ravaging maiden of the Sicilian deep, what manners headlong Hadria bears to you in your course, what peace there is in the Carpathian, with what breeze Doris carries you up, flattered by the thefts of the Agenorean bull? But I have deserved my complaints. For why, when you sought the camp, did I not go, an eager comrade, even to the unknown Indians and Cimmerian chaos? My king's warlike standards would stand near, whether you held weapons in your hand or the reins, or gave laws to the armed; and of your works, though not a partner, surely an admirer I would be present. If once Phoenix, reverend to great Achilles, came to the Ilian shore and Thymbraean Pergamus, unwarlike and sworn to nothing for the swelling son of Atreus, why is my love a coward? But with faithful heart I shall never be absent, and shall follow your sails with long vows. Isis, once stabled beneath the caves of Phoroneus, now queen of Pharos and divinity of the panting East, receive with many-sounding sistrum the Mareotic ship, and the excellent young man, to whom the Latin leader gave the Eastern standards and the Palestinian cohorts to rein, yourself with calm hand lead through the festive thresholds and the sacred harbours and your cities. With you as guide let him learn whence comes the fertile licence of the marshy Nile, why the shoals subside and the bank confines the waters that are pooled with Cecropian mud, why grudging Memphis, or why the mouth of Therapnaean Canopus is wanton, why the Lethean doorkeeper guards the Egyptian altars, why cheap animals are equal to the great gods; what altars the long-lived Phoenix spreads for itself, what fields it deigns, or in what flood of Nile the adored Apis plunges, to the alarm of trembling shepherds. Lead him too to the Emathian shades, where the warlike founder of the city, drenched with Hyblaean nectar, endures, and the serpent-bearing house, where, sunk in coaxing poison, the Actian Cleopatra fled the Ausonian chains.
