On even to the Assyrian seats and the appointed camps escort him, and to Latin Mars, goddess, hand over the young man, nor will he be a new guest: as a boy he sweated in these fields, known as yet only by the light of the broader stripe, yet brave already to outstrip the squadrons with an easy wheel and to condemn the Eastern arrows with his javelin. Therefore there shall be that day, on which, about to give you greater things, Caesar shall bid you depart from your finished war, and we, again standing on this shore, shall behold the vast waves and shall beg for other breezes. O how great I shall be then, or how great the votive lyre I shall move with my quill! When, my neck bound with a great band, you lift me on your shoulders, and first upon my breast, new from the ship, you lean, and give back the kept conversations, and in turn we tell of the years between: you of swift Euphrates and royal Bactra and the sacred wealth of ancient Babylon and Zeugma, the road of the Latin peace, how sweet the grove of flowering Idyme, where precious Tyre reddens, with what juice the purple of Sidon is twice dyed in the vats, where in their first bud the white twigs sweat out the lucky balsam: but I, what tombs I gave to the conquered Pelasgians, or what page shall close for me my laboured Thebes.
A Thanksgiving to the Emperor Augustus Germanicus Domitian The royal banquets of Sidonian Dido one poet praises,
he who brought great Aeneas to the Laurentian fields;
another sets forth the feast of Alcinous in enduring song,
he who wore out Ulysses returning over the wide sea:
but I, to whom Caesar has given new joys of the sacred feast
now first, and to rise at the lord's table,
with what lyre shall I celebrate my prayers? what thanks shall I
be enough to render? Not if at once both Smyrna and Mantua
should twine fragrant laurels about my exalted brow
could I speak worthily; I seem to recline amid the very stars
with Jove, and from the hand of Trojan Ganymede to take
the wine of immortality! Barren were the years I let pass:
this is the first day of my life for me, this the threshold of being.
Is it you, ruler of the lands and great parent
of the conquered world, you, the hope of men, you, the care of the gods,
whom I behold as I lie here? Is it given to gaze upon that face
near at hand, amid the wines and the feast, and not to rise?
A roof august, immense, distinguished not by a hundred columns,
but by as many as could uphold the gods above
and the heavens, were Atlas released from his burden. The neighbouring
palace of the Thunderer stands amazed, and the powers rejoice
that you are set in a seat their equal; nor hurry to climb the great heaven;
so vast spreads the pile, so free the sweep of the spreading hall,
freer than the open field, embracing much of the covered
upper air, and only less than its lord: he fills
the household, and gladdens it with his mighty presence; there rivalling,
the African mountain and the gleaming Trojan, and much Syene,
and Chios, and the marble that vies with grey-green Doris,
and Luna, sufficient only for the bearing of columns.
The view stretches high above: weary eyes can scarcely
grasp the summits, and you would think it the panelled ceiling of golden heaven.
Here Caesar bade the lords of Romulus and the robed
ranks, a thousand at once, recline at his tables together,
Ceres herself, her robe girt up, and Bacchus labour
to suffice; thus happily flowed the heavenly course
of Triptolemus; thus beneath the vine-bearing shoot Lyaeus
shaded the bare hills and the sober fields.
But for me it was not the feast, nor the timbers of Moorish wood
leaning on Indian columns, nor the throngs of attendants in order,
but to gaze upon him alone, him alone, that my desire
had leisure—his face tranquil, with serene majesty
softening his rays and modestly lowering
the standards of his fortune; yet on his countenance there shone
an honour he sought to hide; such even a barbarian foe
could behold and own, and nations that knew him not.
Not otherwise does Gradivus recline in the cold valley
of Rhodope, his horses unyoked; thus Pollux lays down
his supple limbs, loosened from the Therapnaean wrestling-ground;
thus Euhan lies by the Ganges amid the howling Indians;
thus Alcides, weighed down, returning from his grim labours,
rejoiced to lean his side upon the outstretched lion-skin.
I speak of little things, and do not yet match your face, Germanicus:
such, when he revisits the bound of Ocean and the tables
of the Ethiopians, his face suffused with sacred nectar,
the lord of the gods bids the Muses sing their secret songs
and Phoebus praise the triumphs of Pallene.
May the gods—for the lesser souls, they say, are often heard—
grant you to pass the bounds of your country's age
twice and thrice over! May the powers be fixed for our wretched stars,
may you grant temples and dwell in our homes! Often may you open
the yearly thresholds, often salute Janus with a new lictor,
often renew the lustres of five years with garlanded ceremonies!
Since you have given me a happy feast and the sacred rites
of your table, such a day, after long time, has come
to me as that beneath the hills of Trojan Alba,
when, while you sang now of German lines of battle, now of the loud
combats of Dacia, your hand clothed me in Pallas's gold.
Praises of Crispinus, Son of Vettius Bolanus My friend Crispinus seeks the Tyrrhenian countryside and the glades of Tages;
nor is the delay long, nor the land remote,
but my heart is plucked by a secret bite,
and my moist eyes drive forth swelling drops,
as if over the Aegean storms I followed the sails
of a departing friend, and watched his ship, weary now from the high
cliffs, and complained that my eyes were beaten by the long expanse of air.
What, if the bright beginnings of a first campaign
and the sweet auspice of the camp now called you,
distinguished boy, with how much weeping would my joys flow,
what embraces would I give! Are even sad things to be desired
by kindred? And twice eight orbits your life
has now circled. But your spirit is sturdier than your narrow years,
and bends beneath the burden, and your age does not contain its own mind;
no wonder: no inglorious line of forebears,
obscure in ancestors and lacking the light of old,
bore you from plebeian stock; not sprung from squadron-blood,
new to the trabea and with a poor stripe,
did you, a stranger, knock at the august seat and the inner shrine
of the Latian senate, but with the line of your own people
going before; as through the acres of the Romulean circus,
when, fair to see and noble in his ancestral titles,
a horse is awaited, from whose long pedigree
the lucky stud-farm has parents that have well deserved,
him all the applause spurs on, him the very dust
as he flies, and the curving turning-posts, rejoice to recognize:
so you, bright boy, the senate-house felt to be born for itself,
and the patrician moon enclosed your first steps.
Soon your shoulders, by custom, knew the Tyrian folds
and the powerful tunic; but indeed a great father was preparing
great examples for your titles, since he, entering his youth
at once, warlike, invaded the quivered Araxes
and Armenia, hard to teach to serve fierce Nero;
Corbulo wielded the chief command of rigid Mars,
but as companion of the war and sharer of its toils
he too, much admiring him in his distinguished arms,
took Bolanus; and to him, accustomed to entrust the harshest
of his cares and to share his fears: what time was friendly
to stratagems, what good times there were when war was unsheathed,
what faith was suspect, or what was the true flight of the fierce
Armenian. Bolanus to foreknow the road to be feared,
Bolanus to seek ridges fit for a safe camp,
Bolanus to measure the fields, to open the grudging
delays of torrents and woods, and to fill the great mind
of the awesome leader, and alone to suffice
for the huge commands. The barbarian land itself already knew the man;
he was the second peak of the wars, the helmet next to the chief,
as the Phrygians, astonished, though they saw the Nemean
arms and the Cleonaean bow driving the battle-lines,
while Alcides fought, yet feared Telamon too.
Learn, boy—for not from a stranger's counsel must you seek
the fair love of virtue: let kindred praise furnish your spirit;
to others let the Decii and the returning Camilli
be shown—do you learn your father, how great, bearing his orders,
he entered Thule, which denies itself to the western
waves and to wearied Hyperion, and how great he ruled,
allotted for a year, the thousand cities of mighty Asia,
his sway softened by the toga. Drink such things with attentive
ears; let your kinsmen vie to commend these to you,
let your companions and your father's old men repeat these precepts.
And now you prepare another journey, nor with idle step
do you mean to go; not yet have the marks of sturdy youth
crept upon your cheeks, and still the course of your life is unbroken,
nor is your father near; for, drained by unjust fates,
he died, leaving a twofold offspring without a guardian.
Nor at least from your tender arms did the boyish purple
slip off, and the white mantle clothe your shoulders,
whom no unbridled youth corrupted, nor the freedom
of the new toga, taken too soon! As a wood that knows not the sickle
lifts its foliage and breathes out its fruit in shade.
But for you Pierian cares beneath your tender breast,
and modesty, and learned manners that prescribe their own law to themselves;
then glad uprightness and a tranquil brow and a brightness
that holds the border of luxury, and devotion dispensed
through every measure; to yield to your coeval brother,
to admire your father and forgive your wretched mother,
the fortune of your house warned you. Could she have prepared
for you those abominable cups and deadly juices with her hand,
you who by your voice can turn aside the bites
of serpents and appease all stepmothers with your face?
It is right to harass the shades and rightly by curse
to take away the peace of the pyre; but you, best of boys, I see
turning your gaze and preparing such words:
'Spare, I pray, the ashes: that was fate and the wrath of the guilty
Parcae and the crime of a god, who sees mortal
hearts too late, nor at the first threshold checks
the attempts of crimes and minds preparing unspeakable things.
Let that day pass from time, nor let later
ages believe it! Let us at least be silent and suffer
the crimes of our own race to be covered, buried in deep
night. He has exacted the penalty, he whose care is for his own people,
by whose authorship Devotion returns and revisits the earth,
whom every wickedness fears; enough is this vengeance, to be wept by us;
would that it were permitted to entreat the savage
Furies and turn aside Cerberus from the timid shade
and give swiftly to her spirit the forgetful stream of the dead.'
Blessing on your spirit, young man! But the mother's crimes grow,
nor was it only devotion, but at once steep virtue
that you affected. Lately, when by chance a companion
grew pale at the false charge of an undeserving repute,
and the Forum was roused, and, girt with many a judge,
it rose, and Julia brandished her chaste thunderbolt:
you, though you had not before endured the Forum and the stern
laws, but lay hidden in the silent shade of study,
took it upon you to defend his fears and to ward off
the hostile darts, unarmed still and a recruit, for a trembling friend.
Never did Romulus or the Dardanian old man behold
such years warring in the gowned slaughter
of the midmost Forum. The fathers were amazed at such great attempts
and your endeavours, nor did the defendant himself fear you.
Equal vigour is in your limbs, and strength prompt for brave deeds
suffices your spirit and follows its vast commands.
I myself lately saw you on the Tiberine shore,
where the Tyrrhenian wave seethes in the Laurentine shallows,
driving your course and vexing the bare flanks
of a fierce horse with your heel, in face and right hand threatening:
—if there is any faith in words, I was amazed and thought you armed—:
so, fair on his Gaetulian horse and shaking his Trojan
weapons, the hunter Ascanius went into his stepmother's
fields, and burned for wretched Elissa for his father's sake;
not otherwise Troilus with lighter circle baffled
the threatening horses, or he whom from the high towers,
as he wheeled the Arcadians round the turning-posts in the Ogygian dust,
the Tyrian mothers watched with no grim eye.
Therefore come now—the leader's indulgence urges you
and your glad brother gives sure footprints to your prayers—
rise in spirit and conceive the brave cares of the camp.
Mars and the Attic maiden will show you battle-lines,
Castor to turn horses, Quirinus to shake arms on your shoulders,
he who allowed you, on a neck so tender,
to clash the cloud-born shields and the arms untouched by slaughter.
What lands, then, into what world of Caesar will you go?
Will you swim the northern rivers and the broken streams
of the Rhine, or will you sweat in the heat-bearing fields of Libya?
Or will you shake the ridges of Pannonia and the Sauromatae
who change their homes? Or will the sevenfold Hister hold you,
and Peuce, flowed round by her shady consort?
Or will you enter the Solyman ashes and the captured palm-groves,
the woods not happy for itself by the portents of Idume?
But if the land bridled for your great father
receives you, how the fierce Araxes will exult!
What glory will lift the Caledonian fields,
when the long-lived dweller of that savage land shall tell you:
'Here your father was wont to give laws, from this turf to address
his squadrons; far off these watch-towers and forts
—do you see?—he set, and girt these walls with a ditch;
these gifts, these weapons he dedicated to the warlike gods
—you still see the titles—; this breastplate he himself put on
at the call of arms, this he snatched from a British king.'
Just as, to Pyrrhus preparing victorious war against the Teucrians,
Phoenix told of Achilles, unknown to him.
Happy you, who, trusting in your green youth, Optatus,
will endure whatever roads and enter whatever rampart,
perhaps yourself at his side—so may the prince's powers attend—
girt, and a tireless companion of your like-souled friend,
as Pylades was after the pious custom, as the son of Menoetius
waged the Dardanian wars. For this concord is yours,
this love; and may it last, I pray! From me a stronger age
now flees; hence with vows and prayers I will aid his spirit,
and my own! But if perchance I rouse my wonted laments
and the fathers of Romulus come to my songs,
you, Crispinus, will be wanting to me, and through every tier
my Achilles will look round for you, absent.
But you will come back better—the bards' omens do not run
in vain—. And he who now opens to you the eagles and the camp,
the same will grant you to pass through all the ranks and be girt
with the proud fasces and to sit on your fathers' curule chairs.
But who from the lofty hills of Trojan Alba,
whence that god, nearest, looks out upon the walls
of his Rome close by, enters swifter than Fame,
a messenger, and fills your home, Crispinus?
Surely I said: the bards' auguries do not run
in vain; behold! Caesar unbars to you the vast threshold of honours
and entrusts to you the duties of Ausonian iron.
Go, boy, and striving suffice for such great gifts,
happy, you who now swear beneath a great commander,
and to whom sacred Germanicus first hands the sword!
This is no less than if the Lord of War himself unfolded to you
the eagles, brave one, and drew over you the grim face
of the helmet. Go, eager, and learn to deserve greater things!

The Tiburtine Villa of Manilius Vopiscus If anyone has been able to behold the chilly Tibur of eloquent Vopiscus, and his twin dwellings with the Anio set between, or to know the commerce of the kindred bank and the villas vying with each other to claim their lord, on him Sirius never barked with its hot star, nor did the cub of leafy Nemea look fiercely: such is the winter under that roof; so do the kindly frosts break the sun, and the house does not swelter through the Pisaean year. With her own tender hand Pleasure herself wrote there beside you, then Venus anointed the gables with Idalian juices and stroked them with her hair, and left a coaxing grace upon the seat, and forbade her winged sons to depart. O day to be remembered long! What joys I bring back in my mind, what wonders that wearied my sight! How gentle the genius of the ground! What beauty in those blessed places, before hands and art! Nowhere did Nature indulge herself more lavishly. The deep groves leaned over the swift shallows: a deceiving image answers back from the leaves, and the same shadow flees down the long waters, the Anio itself—wondrous faith—both below and above here lays aside its swollen fury and foaming murmurs, rocky though it is, as if afraid to disturb calm Vopiscus's Pierian days and his slumbers that hold songs. Each shore is at home, nor does the gentlest stream divide you; the rival mansions keep their banks, and do not complain that anything foreign, or the river, stands between. Now let Fame boast of the Sestian strait and the sea swum across and of the dolphins conquered by the daring youth! Here is eternal quiet, here no rule of storms, never a fever in the waters; here one may pass across glances and voices and almost hands, just as the receding waters thrust back Chalcis. So, sundered by the deep, the Bruttian shore looks across to Sicilian Pelorus. What shall I sing first, what in the middle, where shall I rest? Shall I marvel at the gilded beams, or the Moorish doorposts everywhere, or the marbles bright with their painted vein, or the nymphs let into every chamber? Hither by eye, hither by mind I am drawn. Shall I tell of the venerable age of the groves? Of you, hall, who look down upon the river's shallows, or you who look back to the silent woods, where all is rest for you, untouched by any whirlwind, the night falls silent and murmurs invite gentle sleep? Or of the baths that steam, set on a grassy ledge, and the fire laid upon the cold banks? And of the stream joined to the steaming furnaces, that laughs at the panting nymphs in the neighbouring river? I have seen the arts and hands of the ancients, and metals alive in their various modes; it is a labour to recall the figures of gold, or the ivory, or the gems worthy to touch one's fingers, and all that silver first, or in lesser bronze, has played at, and the hand that has tried its skill on giant colossi. As I wander with my gaze and draw my eyes over everything, I was treading unawares on riches. For a splendour, flowing down from above, and tiles that gave back the bright bronze revealed the floor, where, painted with varied arts, the ground rejoices and outdoes the unswept floor with new figures: my steps took fright. Why should I now marvel at the linked or the parted houses, kept apart by their three chambers? Or at you, the tree saved in the midst of the dwelling, who through roof and posts come forth into the liquid air— under no master destined to suffer the cruel axe? And now perhaps, unknowing, a slippery Naiad or a Hamadryad owes you years not cut short. Why should I tell of the alternating tables above the twin mound, and the whitening pools and the deep fountains in the flood, and you, Marcia, who glide far within across the slanting stream and run over the river by a daring leaden conduit? Or shall a sweet path lead Elis's river alone beneath the Ionian waves down to the Aetnaean harbours? There the Anio himself, leaving his caves and spring, under the secret night, having stripped off his grey-green mantle, stretches his breast here and there upon the fragile moss, or falls headlong into the pools and claps the glassy waters with his swimming, while Tiburnus reclines in that shade, and there Albula longs to plunge her sulphurous locks: this house could draw woodland Phoebe away from Egeria and widow chilly Taygetus of its Dryad choirs and summon Pan from the Lycaean woods. And had the Tirynthian temple not given other lots, the Praenestine sisters too might have moved here. Why should I praise the wild orchards of Alcinous, and you, branches, who never go up empty into the air? Let the acres of Telegonus give way, let the Laurentine fields of Turnus, and the Lucrine dwellings, and the shore of bloody Antiphates; let the treacherous heights of glassy Circe give way, wailed over by Dulichian wolves, and the citadel of proud Anxur, and the seat that gentle to her Phrygian foster-son the old woman owes; let those shores give way that the rainy storm will call you back to from the Antian coast in deep midwinter. Surely it is here that those famous habits weigh their meditations, here that fertile quiet is pressed, and virtue grave with serene brow, and a sane brightness, and delights without luxury, which the aged Gargettian himself, leaving his own Athens, would prefer to his deserted garden: worth seeking through Aegean winters and the snowy star of the Hyades and under the Olenian signs, if a ship must be trusted to Malea and the way must lie through Sicilian seas: why does a near pleasure seem mean to your eyes? Here your lyre delights the Tiburtine Fauns and Alcides himself and Catillus sung with a greater lyre, whether your spirit would contend with Pindaric quills, or raise the lyre to heroic strength, or trouble with black rust the livid satire, or whether your letter shines with no other care. Worthy of the wealth of Midas and Croesus and of Persian treasure, a blessing on the goods of your mind—you for whom Hermus too should have run across his standing fields with his golden banks and Tagus with his glittering silt! So, plying often your learned leisure, so, your breast cleared of every cloud, I pray you may pass the bound of Nestor's old age.

The Tree of Atedius Melior There stands a tree, shading the clear waters of bright Melior, having clasped the pool, which, from its lowest trunk curved over the shallows, returns thence with upright top, lofty, as though it were born again from the midst of the waves and inhabited the glassy stream with silent roots. Why should I ask Phoebus for so small a thing? Do you tell the causes, Naiads, and you kindly Fauns—enough—give me songs. The tender troops of the nymphs were fleeing Pan; he indeed goes, as if he wished them all, and yet one above all, Pholoe. She, fleeing through woods and rivers, now avoids his hairy steps, now his shameless horns, and now through the warlike grove of Janus and the dark fields of Cacus, and through the Quirinal lands, suspended in flight, she enters the Caelian wastes; there at last, conquered by toil, worn out by fear, where now the open home of calm Melior stands without deceit, she gathered her tawny garments more closely and laid herself down on the edge of the snowy bank. The swift god of the flocks follows, and believes his union already his; with burning breast he poises his sighing at her door, now lightly looms over his prey, when, lo, Diana turns her hurrying steps thither, while through the seven hills she wanders and gathers the tracks of the Aventine deer. She repented of having seen the goddess, and, turning to her faithful companions: 'Shall I never bar from its greedy plunders this wanton and foul herd, and shall the band of my chaste chorus ever dwindle for me?' So, having spoken, she draws from her quiver a short shaft, which she hurls neither with bent horns nor with its wonted whirring, but with one contented hand sent it forth, and the arrow is said to have touched, turned away, the left hand of the sleeping Naiad. She, rising, saw at once the day and the wanton foe, and, lest she should spread her snowy limbs to view, fell so, with all her clothing, into the fountain, and beneath the deep pools, believing Pan pursued, wraps her side in the deep weed. What should the robber do, suddenly cheated? Nor does he dare to trust his body to the deep waters, conscious of his hairy hide, and from his tender years unskilled in swimming: complaining of all, of pitiless Bromius, of the envious pools and the envious shaft, he set down beside it a plane-tree, young to the sight, with long shoot and countless arms and a top destined for the air, and heaped living sand beside, and sprinkled it with the wished-for waters, and gives it such charges: 'Live long, memorable pledge of my vow, tree, and these hidden chambers of the hard nymph do you at least, leaning over, love, and press your leaves upon the water. She indeed deserved it, but let her not, I pray, swelter in the heat from above, nor be struck by hard hail; only remember to sprinkle the water and stir it with your leaves. Then I will long honour you and the mistress of the kindly seat, and will keep both safe in unharmed old age, that, like the leaves of Jove and Phoebus, like the two-coloured shade of the poplar, my pines too may marvel at your shoots.' So he spoke. The tree, animated by the god's old fires, hangs over the teeming pools with slanting trunk and broods, and with loving shadows searches the waters, and hopes for embraces; but the breath of the waters keeps it off and suffers no touch. At last, struggling up to the air, it balances from the bottom, and again ingeniously lifts its knotless top, as though it would descend with another stem into the deepest pools. Now neither does the Phoebean Naiad hate it, but invites with her flood the shut-out branches. These small gifts on your birthday we make ready for you—but to live, perhaps, under a mighty age. You, in whose calm breast have set their seat a coaxing honour and a cheerfulness yet weighty with virtue, to whom is neither slothful quiet nor unjust power nor shameless hope, but a middle path through the honourable and the sweet, incorrupt in faith and untried by any tumults and reserved, while openly you order your life by rule, the same easy despiser of gold and the same most fit to adorn riches and let light into your wealth: in this long flowering youth of mind and character persist to equal the men of Ilium and surpass them, the years that the father bore to Elysium, that the mother bore: this the hard Sisters granted to their prayers, this—the lofty glory of great-souled Blaesus, which, set under your witness and about to flee you in your silence, shall grow green again.

Consolation to Claudius Etruscus Highest of the gods, Piety, whose most welcome power, rare in heaven, looks upon the profaned lands, hither, your hair filleted and distinguished by a snowy robe, such as, present still and driven out by no fraud of the guilty, you dwelt among rude peoples and golden realms, come to the gentle obsequies, and behold the pious tears of mourning Etruscus, and wipe his praised eyes. For who, seeing him break his breast with unfilled lament and embrace the pyre and lean upon the embers, would not believe that the funeral of a young wife was bewailed, or that the face of a son just growing to manhood was snatched away by the flames? It is a father who is wept. Be present, gods and men, at the rites; far hence, far go you guilty, if any have an unspoken crime in their heart, and the long old age of a wearied father, if any is conscious of a struck mother and fears stern Aeacus at the infernal urn: the innocent and chaste I call. See, he holds the aged face gently clasped, and sprinkles his parent's holy gray hair with tears, and loves the soul's last cold; the son thinks his father's swift years —wondrous faith!—and the dark Sisters made too much haste. Exult, calm shades, by the Lethean streams, rejoice, Elysian houses; lay garlands on the altars and let festal altars gladden the pale groves. Happy, this shade, too happy and wept by a son, comes; far off the hisses of the Furies, far off the threefold warder; let the long way open wide within for excellent souls, let him go, and approach the dread throne of the silent lord, and bear his last thanks, and anxiously ask for the young man as many years. A blessing on your pious groaning! We will give solace to worthy mournings, and of our own accord we will hallow to your old man Aonian rites of the dead, Etruscus! Lavish, plunge the Eastern seeds, the proud harvests of Cilicia and Araby, into the pyre; let the fire carry the heir's wealth, and from the high mound let the cinders be packed, that will send pious clouds to the bright sky: we will bring gifts that will not burn, and your sorrow, with me to teach it, will endure into the coming years. For it is not unknown to me to weep a parent; I groaned in like fashion, flung down by the fire. That day urges me to soothe your losses with song: and I myself bore the complaints I now bring to you. Not bright indeed, most gentle old man, was the line of your race, nor a pedigree handed down from forebears, but a great fortune supplied the lack of birth and hid the fault of your parents. For you bore no masters from the commons, but those whom alike the West and the East serve, nor is that a shame to you: for what, on earth and in heaven, remains without the law of obeying? By turns all things are ruled and press one another by turns: every land is under its own kings; happy Rome presses the diadems of kings; to leaders it is given to rein her; soon their power grows over the gods above, but even the divinities have a law: the swift choir of the stars serves, and the wandering moon serves, nor does the orbit of light return so many times unbidden; and—if it be lawful now to match low things with high— the Tirynthian too endured the harsh covenants of a savage king, nor did the pipe of Phoebus, in service, blush. But neither were you sent to Latium from barbarian shores: Smyrna was your native soil, and the harbour with its reverend spring, Meles, and the ford of Hermus, where Lydian Bacchus enters and refreshes his horns in the golden mud. Thence a glad sequence, and from various cares in order honour increased; ever to walk near the divine powers, ever to attend the side of Caesar and to cling to the gods' sacred mysteries was granted. The Tiberian hall first, your face scarce yet imitating a new youth, is opened to you—here freedom, your years overcome by much native worth, came offered—nor did the next heir, though pitiless and driven by the Furies, drive you away. With him too, a slender comrade even to the Arctic frosts, you endured a tyrant dreadful in speech and look, monstrous to his own, like those who tame the dreaded hearts of beasts and bid them, when blood is now tasted, give back the hands plunged in their mouths and live by no prey. But by your merit you rose to chief deeds when Claudius, an old man not yet dismissed to the starry axis, passed you on to be held by a far-off heir. Who, fearing the gods above, is granted to have deserved at once so many temples, so many altars? The winged Arcadian is the messenger of highest Jove; Juno wins the rain-bearing daughter of Thaumas; swift Triton stands ready in obedience to Neptune's commands: you so many times bore in due rite the changed yokes of leaders, unimpaired, and your bark was happy in every deep. And now the high day entered the pious house and Fortune, exalted, came in with full stride; now to you alone is entrusted the ordering of sacred wealth and the riches gathered through all peoples and the expenses of the great world, whatever Iberia casts out from her gold-bearing trenches, what gleams on the Dalmatian mountain, what is swept from the African harvests, whatever the floor of the sweltering Nile grinds, and what the diver, sunk in the Eastern sea, gathers, and the tilled flocks of Lacedaemonian Galaesus and the clear snows and the Massylian timbers and the honour of Indian ivory: to you alone, the trusted minister, all things obey that Boreas and fierce Eurus and cloudy Auster bring in: sooner could you count the winter rains and the leaves of the woods. The same, watchful and of keen mind and swift, unrolls how much under every Roman standard by the day, and how much for the tribes, what the temples, what the high courses of the waters, what the sea's defences require, or the long stretched-out line of the roads; what gold gleams on the lord's lofty ceilings, what mass must melt, to be shaped by fire into the faces of gods, what stamp of Ausonian Moneta rings out in the fire. Hence for you a rare rest, and pleasure shut from your mind, and scant feasts and care never hurt by deep unmixed wine; yet genial laws are dear to your heart, and to bind your mind with bridal couches and to join festive weddings and to beget faithful clients for your lord. Who would not know the lofty stock and the beauty of famous Etrusca? Though by my own eyes she was not known to me, yet a portrait gives back to fame her surpassing grace, and the like beauty of her children shows it in their faces, nor was her stock common; a brother bore the rods and the highest curule chair and the Ausonian swords, and faithful carried the appointed standards, when first the savage madness drove the fierce Dacians on, and the race was condemned in a great triumph. So whatever from her father's blood was lacking, the mother restored, and the house, rejoicing in the marriage, saw the obscure side grow bright; nor were the pledges far off; for twice Lucina came to the births, and with light hand herself, fertile, touched the heavy labours. Happy—ah!—if a long day, if the just threads had granted you to behold the faces of your children and their green cheeks! But the joys fell broken in mid youth, and Atropos cut with her hand the flowering years; as the pale lilies droop their stalks and the budding roses die at the first south winds, or where the new purple breathes out its bloom in the spring meadows. Around those funerals you, arrow-bearing Loves, hovered, and anointed the pyres with the mother's balsam; and there was no measure either with your torn wings or your hair to scatter the fire, and the gathered quivers built the pyre. What rites of the dead then, or what laments would you have given to your mother's pyre, Etruscus, you who think your father's funeral not ripe, and these years untimely for the pious! Him too, who now with his nod tempers the high citadels, sharing his bright offspring with the lands and the stars, gladly endowed with the honour of an Idumaean triumph, and, deeming him worthy of a place in the order of the victorious procession, forbade it not, and his humble parents diminished nothing, and the same led him down to the equestrian rows and changed his station and stripped the ignoble iron from his left hand and matched the honour of his sons. Twice eight lustres flowed for his right hand, and a course of life without a cloud, how rich for the uses of his children, and willing to depart from his whole wealth— witness still the splendour of lavish Etruscus, drawn from there, to whom your indulgence gave manners not lowly. For with embraces ever calling you back you held him, coaxing, and never a father by command; to his honour the brother himself too, more inclined, rejoiced to yield. What thanks do the devoted young men render you for their reborn father, highest of leaders, or what pious vows! You—whether old age, slow with mould and drained of affairs, erred, or whether coaxing Fortune long preferred his return—were content only to warn the old man, astonished and shuddering at the stroke of the thunderbolt to come, with thunder and a gentle storm; and when, beyond the horrid seas of cares, the partner went far off, leaving the Italian fields, he was bidden to withdraw to the soft shores of the Campanian coast and the Diomedean citadels, and was a guest, not an exile. Nor, long delaying, do you, Germanicus, unbar again the Romulean threshold and cherish the mourner and raise his fallen household. No wonder, most gentle leader, since this is that clemency which gives the Cattians, conquered, sparing covenants, and gives the Dacians their own mountain, which lately, after the horrid wars, did not deem the Marcomani and the wandering Sauromatae worthy of a Latin triumph. And now the day is at its end, and the inexorable measure fails. Here the devotion of sad Etruscus demands of me such songs as neither the Sicilian rocks command nor the swan now sure of its fate, nor the wife of savage Tereus. Alas, with what beatings I saw him wearying his arms, and poured out, face down, over the kisses! Scarce do servants and companions hold him, scarce the high fire drives him off. Not otherwise did Theseus groan along the Sunian shores, who had deceived Aegeus with false sails. Then, groaning fearfully and his face fouled, he addresses the warm cinders: 'Why do you leave us, most faithful one, with Fortune returning, father? But now we appeased the powers of the great patron and the brief wraths of the gods above, and you enjoy them not, and, robbed of the use of so great a gift, you flee to the shades, ungrateful, nor is it given to bend the Fates as to appease the harsh powers of evil Lethe. Happy he to whom, bearing his father on his great neck, the sacred reverence of the Mycenaean flame opened its way! And tender Scipio, who from the savage Carthaginians snatched his father, and the rash devotion of Lydian Lausus. Could even the wife of the Thessalian husband weigh out his death, and the Thracian, suppliant, conquer pitiless Styx? How much better might this be allowed for a father! Yet you shall not be snatched away whole, nor shall I send your funeral far off; here your shades, here within the house I shall keep them: you the guardian and lord of the home; to you shall all your kin obey; I, duly the lesser and ever second, shall pour the constant feasts and cups to your sacred shade, and worship your image; you the bright marble, you the line of learned wax shall give back to me like yourself, now ivory, now tawny gold shall change your face, thence I shall ask the way of manners and the examples of a long life and pious addresses and dreams that will warn me.' As he speaks such words, the father hears with glad sweetness and slowly descends to the pitiless shades, and bears the words to his beloved Etrusca, to tell them. Hail for the last time, gentlest of fathers, and for the last time farewell, who, your son surviving, shall never suffer the sad chaos and the mournful mould of a neglected tomb. Ever shall your altars breathe with fragrant flowers, ever shall the happy urn drink Assyrian liquors and tears, which is the greater honour. Here he shall offer sacrifice to your shade, and from your own land shall raise your tomb, and by his example deserving has consecrated to you our songs too, rejoicing in this also, to have given even cinders to this sepulchre.
The Domitian Way What monstrous din of hard flint and heavy iron
has filled the rocky flank of the Appian Way
that lies near the sea?
Surely no Libyan hordes resound,
nor does a foreign general, restless in perjured war,
shake the Campanian fields;
nor does Nero break the shallows and, with mountains hewn down,
lead in the foul marshes;
but he who crowns the warlike thresholds of Janus
with just laws and with the Forum,
who restores to chaste Ceres the acres long denied
and the sober lands,
who forbids the strong sex to perish
and as censor keeps grown men
from fearing the penalty of a beautiful form,
who gives back to the Capitol its Thunderer
and sets Peace again in her own house,
who decrees for his father's race lights that shall
last for ever, and a Flavian heaven:
he, vexed at the people's sluggish roads
and the fields that hold back every journey,
cuts out the long detours and with a new
bedding makes firm the heavy sands,
glad to have brought the home of the Euboean Sibyl
and the gulfs of Gaurus and the steaming
Baiae near to the seven hills.
Here once the traveller, borne on a single axle,
swayed sluggishly with reeling sway,
and the grudging earth swallowed the wheels,
and the Latin folk in the middle of the plains
shuddered at the evils of a voyage;
nor were there nimble courses, but the silent ruts
slowed the impeded journey,
while the languid team, complaining of its too-heavy load,
crept beneath the high yoke-beam.
But now what wore out a whole solid day
has become a journey of scarce two hours;
not the stretched wings of birds through the stars,
nor you, ships, will go more swiftly.
Here was the first labour, to begin the furrows
and cut the boundaries and deeply
hollow out the earth with high heaping;
then to fill the dug trenches again with other matter
and prepare a bed upon the topmost ridge,
lest the ground sink, lest a treacherous footing
give an uncertain couch to the pressed stones;
then with kerbstones forced in on this side and that,
and frequent bolts, to bind the road together.
O how many hands labour at once together!
these cut the wood and strip the mountains,
these lift the rocks and beams with iron;
those bind the stones and weave the work
with baked dust and dirty tufa;
these drain the thirsty pools by hand
and drive the lesser streams far off.
These right hands could hollow out even Athos,
and could shut off the mournful sea of groaning Helle
with a bridge that does not float.
By these the little Inous Isthmus, did the gods not forbid the passage,
would have mingled the straits.
The shores grow hot, and the moving woods;
a long crash goes through the cities between,
and at once on this side and on that the broken echo
vine-bearing Massicus sends back to Gaurus;
quiet Cyme marvels at the sound,
and the Liternan marsh, and the sluggish Savo.
But Vulturnus, his tawny head and his dripping
hair entangled far with soft sedges,
lifts his face, and reclined upon the great
arch of Caesar's bridge
pours forth such words from his hoarse throat:
'Good founder of my fields,
who bound me, poured back into trackless valleys
and not knowing how to keep my banks,
with the laws of a straight channel,
and now I, that turbid and threatening one,
scarcely suffering doubtful boats before,
now bear a bridge and am crossed on foot;
I who was wont to snatch lands and whirl forests
away—it shames me!—have begun to be a river;
but I give thanks, and such servitude is worth so much,
that under you as leader, at your command, I yielded,
that you, the greatest arbiter and perpetual
victor of my bank, chose me;
and now you grace me with a blessed channel
and do not let me grow foul, and far off
wipe away the shame of the barren soil,
lest, dusty and heavy with mist,
the gulf of the Tyrrhenian deep should wash over me,
such as Cinyphian Bagrada, while the bank is silent,
creeps along between the Punic fields;
but let me be borne such that with shining course
I may challenge the calm sea and the neighbouring
Liris with my clear flood.'
So spoke the river, and at the same time he had raised
with his vast back the marble-paved expanse;
the gate and prosperous threshold of this road
is an arch, gleaming with the warlike trophies of the leader
and with all the metals of the Ligurians,
as great as that which crowns the clouds with rain.
There the roused traveller is turned aside,
there the Appian grieves to be left behind;
then the course is swifter and keener,
then the very onset delights the yoked teams;
as when, the rowers' arms being weary,
the first breezes flutter the sails,
so come, then, all you who beneath the first sky
honour the faith of the Roman parent,
travel down the sloping road, you nations,
come more swiftly, you laurels of the East.
Nothing stands against the eager, nothing delays:
he who leaves the Tiber at the first dawn
may sail the Lucrine at the first evening.
But near the lowest end of the new road,
where Apollo points to ancient Cumae,
I see one white with hair and fillets!
Are my eyes deceived? Or does the Sibyl
bring forth from the sacred caves her Chalcidian laurels?
Let us give way; lyre, now lay aside your songs:
a holier seer begins; we must be silent.
Behold! she turns her neck, and far through the new
spaces revels, and fills the road,
then thus speaks with maiden mouth:
'I was saying, he will come—wait, you fields
and river—he will come, with heaven favouring,
who will lift the foul grove and the rotting sands
with lofty bridges and a road.
Behold! here is the god; him Jupiter bids
rule the blessed lands in his stead;
than whom none worthier takes up these reins
since I as guide led prescient Aeneas,
eagerly seeking the future of Avernus,
into the groves, and he entered them and left them again.
He is good in peace, he is to be feared in arms,
better than Nature and more powerful.
If he held the flaming axles,
with generous clouds you would be drenched, India;
Libya would be flooded, Haemus would grow warm.
Hail, leader of men and parent of the gods,
godhead foreseen and stored up for me.
No longer unrolled from rotting scrolls
with the solemn prayer of the fifteen men
scan my words, but hear me singing
face to face, as you deserve.
I have seen what chain of deserving years
the bright sisters spin forth for you:
a great order of ages awaits you,
longer than your sons and your sons' grandsons.
You will pass your years in perpetual youth,
those peaceful years which Nestor is said to have reached,
which the old age of Tithonus counts,
and as many as I asked of the Delian god.
Already the snowy Bear has sworn to you;
now the East will give you great triumphs.
You will go where wandering Hercules and Euhan went,
beyond the stars and the flaming sun
and the source of the Nile and the snows of Atlas,
and blessed with every heaping of praises
you will mount, as warrior, and refuse the triumphal car;
until the Trojan fire and the reborn
Tarpeian father shall thunder in his renewed hall,
until this road, while you rule the earth,
shall grow older than the aged Appian.'
A Funeral Lament for His Father Give me yourself those evil powers and a song of lamentation
from the Elysian spring, and the strain of the left-hand
lyre, learned father. For it is not right that the Delian caves
be moved nor wonted Cirrha be stirred
without you. Whatever Phoebus of late in the Corycian shade,
whatever Euhan was showing from the Ismarian hills,
I have unlearned. The Parnassian fleeces have fled my locks,
and I have dreaded—a horror!—the deadly yew creep into the ivy
and the trembling laurel wither.
Surely I, who went to exalt the deeds of great-souled kings,
breathing high and matching Mars in song,
who has cast cold clouds over my barren heart with sluggish
decay, who, Apollo being sunk, over my condemned mind?
The goddesses stand round the thunderstruck bard, sounding nothing
sweet either with fingers or voice; their leader herself, propped with her head
on the silent lyre, as after Orpheus was snatched away
she stood beside you, Hebrus, beholding now the deaf
ranks of beasts and the unmoved groves, the song lifted away.
But you, whether, sent forth from the body, stretching to the heights
you review the gleaming tracts and the elements of things,
what god, whence fires, what path leads the sun,
what diminishes Phoebe, and what cause can restore
her when hidden, and unfold the measures of well-known Aratus,
or whether on the secret grass of the Lethaean field
near the assemblies of heroes and the blessed shades,
the Maeonian and Ascraean old men, no slower a shade
you dwell beside, and sound your verses in turn and mingle songs:
give voice, father, and genius to my great grief,
for me, thrice reading the heaven and thrice unweaving her face,
the Moon sees idle, and consoling sad cares with no
Heliconian art; since your fire glowed for me on those features
and I drank your ashes with weeping eyes,
honour is worthless to my studies; scarcely to these offices
do I first loose my spirit, and to drive decay from my silent
cares now even with sinking hand and with no dry eye
I begin, leaning on the tomb, where you softly rest
holding our acres, where after the death of Aeneas
starry Ascanius heaped upon the Latian mountains his Alba,
while he hated the fields rich with Phrygian blood
and the dotal kingdom of an ill-omened stepmother.
Here I—for the breath of Sicanian saffron does not breathe
more gently, nor if the rare Sabaeans had plucked for you their
cinnamon, nor the Arab his fragrant ears of spice—
you, to be heaped with funeral offerings, I bewail with Pierian
song; take, O take the groans and the wounds of your son
and his tears, such as few parents ever had.
And would that fortune were mine to give altars to your shade,
a work equal to temples, and to raise an airy pile,
beyond the rocks of the Cyclopes and the bold stones
of the Pyramids, and to fringe your tomb with a great grove!
There I would have surpassed the gifts of the Sicilian sepulchre
and the grove of Nemea and the rites of the mangled Pelops.
There the naked strength of Grecian men would not cleave
the air with the Oebalian discus, nor sweat of horses water
the fields, nor the hoof give a sound in the crumbling track;
but a simple chorus of Phoebus, and the leafy
prizes of bards I would duly bind for you, praised father.
Myself with streaming eyes, priest of the shades and the soul,
I would sing first the lament, from which neither Cerberus with all
his mouths nor the laws of Orpheus could turn you away.
And there, singing your manners and deeds,
perhaps fortune would not have ranked me below grand-voiced Homer,
and devotion would strive to match grim Maro.
Why should she more assail the gods above and the bronze threads
of the sisters, the bereaved mother who sits over the warm mound
of her son, or she who looks upon the fire of her young husband
and overcomes the hands that bar her and the throng that holds her,
leaping, ready to die, into the burning man?
Greater perhaps than these I may beat the gods above and Tartarus
with my envy: even to strangers let my funeral go,
pitiable to look upon. But neither now has Nature given herself
to my grieving, nor Devotion to just claim; for me at the first threshold
of fate and in green age, father, snatched as it were from life,
you go down to harsh Tartarus. For not more sparingly did the Marathonian maid
bewail Icarius, slain by the crime of savage rustics,
than the parent her Astyanax, falling from the Phrygian tower,
though that maid shut up her groans in a final
noose: but you, after the funeral of great
Hector, it shames her to have served a Haemonian husband.
Not those laments which, sure of fate, the swan
sends before itself by tuneful death, nor those which from the black rock
the Tyrrhenian birds threaten too sweetly to sailors,
will I bring to my father's pyre: not what with broken murmur
Philomela laments and bewails to her cruel sister:
too well known to a bard. Who has not in his lament named all
the boughs of the Heliades and the tearful buds
and the Phrygian stone, and her who dared songs against
Phoebus, and Pallas not glad of the faithless boxwood?
You let Devotion, forgetful of men, and Justice recalled
from heaven, and Eloquence with twin tongue lament,
and Pallas and the learned Heliconian band of Phoebus,
whose labour is to lead Aonian songs by the six-foot measure,
and those to whom the song on the Arcadian shell, by measures,
was the care of the lyre and its name, and those whom under all the world
steep Wisdom counts by its sevenfold fame,
who over the furies and the houses of kings and the stars
averse from heaven thundered in the terrifying tragic buskin,
and those whose joy it was to make slender their powers with wanton Thalia,
or sweetly to truncate the heroic measures by their step.
For having embraced all in his mind, and master of all
where the broad power of speech lies open, whether it pleased him to bind
his beginnings in Aonian measures, or in loosened speech
to scatter them and match the storm-clouds with unbridled utterance.
Lift up your half-ruined face suddenly from the dust,
Parthenope, and set your hair, buried by the breathing mountain,
over the tombs and the funeral of your great foster-child,
than whom nothing more excellent did the Munychian citadel,
nor learned Cyrene nor spirited Sparta create.
If you lay devoid of lineage and obscure in fame,
holding nothing of your race, by him alone you would prove yourself
Greek and drawn from your ancestors' Euboean blood.
He so often furnished the seasons for your garlands,
when in praised verse he sang the appointed lustres,
surpassing the lips of the Pylian old man and the lips of the king
of Dulichium, his hair bound beneath both wreaths.
Not for you a deformed origin of obscure blood,
nor a race without light (although the fortune of his parents
was straiter than its outlay): for in rich fashion
Infancy chose to lay aside for you your purple robes
given for the honour of your stock, and the noble gold of your breast.
At once, when you were born, the Aonian sisters smiled
propitious, and Apollo, already then kindly to me,
dipped the boy's lyre and his lips in the sacred stream.
Nor is your country's glory single, and your natal origin
hangs on the doubtful contest of two lands.
Greek Hyele, adopted among the Latian colonists, reports you
of her race, where the heavy steersman fell from the ship
and the wretch awoke in the midst of the waves;
but greater from there, by the long order of his life, Parthenope
proves him her own . . . Homer too other cities by other birthplaces
tear apart, and all claim him; he is not true to all,
a monstrous glory of the false nourishes the vanquished.
And there, while you brought forth years and a healthy life,
at once you are swept to the contests of your country's festival,
scarcely to be filled by men, hasty for praise and bold
of talent. The people of Euboea were amazed at your earliest songs,
and parents pointed you out to their sons.
Thence frequent in the contest, and your voice inglorious
at no sacred game: not so often did green Therapnae applaud
Castor as victor in the course, nor his brother with the cestus.
But if it was easy to conquer at home: what to earn the Achaean
prizes, now with Phoebus's branches, now with the grass of Lerna,
now with temples protected by the Athamantean pine,
when, though so often wearied, yet nowhere did far-wandering Victory
bear off your leaves or touch another's locks?
Hence the vows of the fathers were entrusted to you, and the noble youth
ruled by your guidance; to learn the manners and deeds of the men
of old, what was the fall of Troy, how slow Ulysses returned,
how great Homer ran over horses and the battles of men in verse,
and how greatly the Ascraean and the Sicilian old man enriched
the pious countrymen; by what law the curved voice of the Pindaric lyre
runs back, and Ibycus, the suppliant of birds,
and Alcman sung at stern Amyclae,
and fierce Stesichorus, and Sappho rash to have entered
the manly leaps, unafraid of the dread Leucadian rock,
and whatever others the lyre deemed worthy. You, skilled to unfold
the songs of the son of Battus and the hiding-places of Lycophron's art,
and intricate Sophron and the secrets of slender Corinna.
But why do I speak of small things? You, accustomed to bear an equal
yoke with Homer, and to match the six feet with loosened
verses, and never to be left behind by a shorter step,
what wonder, if, leaving their homeland, they sought you,
those whom the Lucanian field, those whom the acres of rigid Daunus,
those whom the house wept by Venus and the land neglected
of Alcides, or those whom from the Surrentine height
the maiden, watcher of the Tyrrhenian deep, sends,
those whom, by a nearer bay, the hill marked by trumpet and oar,
and Cyme, of old the hostess of an Ausonian home,
and those whom the Dicaearchean harbours and the Baian
shores send, where deep amid the waters the fire,
mingled, pants, and the hidden conflagrations guard the homes?
So to the Avernal rocks and the dark caves
of the Sibyl the nations came from everywhere to ask,
and she sang the threats of the gods and the deeds of the Parcae,
a seer not vain, though Phoebus was deceived.
Soon you instruct the Romulean stock and the lords to be,
and persist in leading them in the footsteps of their fathers.
Under you the Dardanian explorer of the hidden fire,
who conceals the inner shrine of the Diomedean theft,
grew, and thence the boy learned the sacred rites; you, as approver of arms,
showed them to the Salii, and the prophetic sky to sure
augurs; to whom it was right to unroll the Chalcidian song,
why the hair of the Phrygian flamen lies hidden, and your
scourges the girt Luperci greatly feared.
And now perhaps from that flock one to the nations
gives laws in the East, another curbs the Spaniards,
another shuts off the Achaemenian Persian by Zeugma,
these bridle the rich peoples of Asia, these the Pontic lands,
these mend the forums with peacemaking fasces, those
hold the camps in pious station: you are the source of their praise.
Not for you would Nestor have vied to mould youthful hearts,
nor Phoenix, the governor of an untamed pupil,
nor Chiron, who broke with another song the son of Aeacus,
willing to hear the keen trumpets and the clarions.
While you celebrate such things, suddenly civil Erinys
moved the torch from the Tarpeian mount and Phlegraean
battles; the Capitol gleams with sacrilegious brands,
and the Latian cohorts took up the furies of the Senones;
scarce was there respite from the flame, nor had that pyre of the gods
yet settled, when you, eager solace for the ruined temples,
and much swifter than the very torches,
in the assemblies with pious lips bewail the captive thunderbolts.
The lords of Latium marvel, and the avenger of the gods,
Caesar, and from the midst of the divine fire the father gives assent.
And now your mind was set to weep with pious song
the Vesuvian fires and to spend a groan on your country's losses,
when the father lifted the mountain, snatched from the lands, to the stars
and far flung it down upon the wretched cities.
Me too, knocking at the tuneful groves and the Boeotian valleys,
when I said I was descended from your stock, the goddesses
admitted; for not only the stars and seas
and lands, which custom owes to a parent, did you give me,
but this glory, whatever it is, of the lyre, and you first gave me
to speak no common thing and to hope for fame from the tomb.
How were you, whenever I soothed the Latian fathers
with my song, and you, a happy spectator, were present
at your gift! Alas, with what weeping was your joy confounded,
amid vows and pious fears and glad shame!
How that day was yours, how no greater was the glory mine!
So when the man who begot him watches the youth
in the Olympian arena, he himself strikes more, more in his deep heart
is he beaten; the tiers attend, but by the Achaeans
he is gazed at more, while again and again he buries his eyes in the dust thrown up
and prays, the crown seized, to expire.
Alas for me, that I bore only my country's leaves on my head
and the Ceres-gifts of the Chalcidian crown alone
with you as witness! How would the Dardanian field of Alba
scarcely have contained you, if through me you had borne the garlands
given by Caesar's hand! What strength would that day
have lent, how much could it have taken from your old age!
For that the oak mingled with olive did not press my brow,
and the hoped-for honour fled: how sweet for my parent
would the trackless heights of the Tarpeian be! With you as master,
my Thebaid was pressing on the beginnings of the bards of old;
you were to spur my songs, you to unfold the deeds
of heroes and the measures of war and the placings of regions
you showed me. My course wavers on an uncertain path
without you, and the sails of my bereaved ship grow dim.
Nor did you cherish me only with bounteous devotion:
such too in the marriage-chamber, one torch known to you,
one wedlock, one love. Surely I cannot now part my mother
from your cold tomb: she feels you and holds you,
she sees you, and salutes the tombs at sunrise and sunset,
as others with feigned devotion tend the Pharian griefs
and the Mygdonian, and bewail funerals not their own.
Why should I tell of your displayed manners, your kept dignity?
What devotion, what cheapness of gain, what care of modesty,
how great a love of right? And again, when it was sweet to relax,
what grace in your words, what no old age in your mind?
For these your deserts, fame and kindly praise
the judging care of the gods granted you, and a life sad with no
wound; you are snatched away, father, not lacking years,
not having too many, bearing thrice ten lustres of years
joined; but devotion and grief do not let me count, O you worthy
to pass the Pylian goals of age and equal the Teucrian
old men, O worthy to see me like yourself! But not for you was the gate
of death sad: for the causes were light, nor did an exit sluggish
with the corruption of old age send your limbs before to the waiting tomb,
but a dull torpor and a death that mimicked rest
unfolded you, and bore you under Tartarus in a false sleep.
What groans I then—the anxious band of companions saw,
your mother saw, and as an example rejoiced and recognized—
what laments I bore! Grant me pardon, shades,
it is right to have said it, father: you would have given me no more.
Happy is he who clasped his father with empty arms:
he would, though placed in the Elysian seat, snatch him away
and bear him again through the Danaan shades;
him, attempting, and forcing his living steps into Tartarus,
the long-lived seer of infernal Diana brought down;
so the cause, a lesser one, sent the Odrysian lyre
across sluggish Avernus; so Admetus on the Thessalian shores:
if one day brought back the Phylacean shade,
why should the lyre, father, entreat nothing, whether yours or mine,
among the shades? May it be right for me so to touch my father's face,
right to have joined hands, and let whatever law follow.
But you, kings of the shades and Ennaean Juno,
if I pray for things worthy of praise, take away the torches and the hair
of the Furies; let the harsh doorkeeper sound with no mouth,
let the averse valleys hide the Centaurs and the herds of Hydra
and the Scyllaean monsters, and let the last ferryman
invite the aged shade to his banks, the throng dispersed,
and gently set him among the central seaweed.
Go, pious shades and swarms of Grecian bards,
and sprinkle the illustrious soul with Lethaean garlands
and show the grove into which no Fury has burst,
in which is false daylight and air most like to heaven.
Thence yet may you come, by the better gate where horn
conquers the malignant ivory, and in the likeness of sleep show the visions
you were wont; as the gentle nymph dictated the sacred rites of Numa
and the worship to be observed, beneath the Arician cave,
as Scipio is believed by the Ausonians to have drawn full sleep
from Latian Jove, as Sulla not without Apollo.

On the Recovery of Rutilius Gallicus You are there, O gods above, nor does Clotho roll her work inexorable: kindly Astraea sees the pious, and reconciled to Jove returns and looks upon the stars she had doubted, Gallicus, you belong to heaven. You, Germanicus the god, hold him dear—who would deny it?—Fortune blushed to strip your empire of so great a minister. There stands a neck close to you, that has cast off a weight immense and the ruinous threads of old age, and grows green again, better, into other years. So let the cohorts that keep the city's standards be eager, and the courts that flee so often, in their tumult, to your bosom with their complaints, the laws and the cities everywhere that wear the toga, that beg your justice with far-off entreaties, let them vie in gladness; and let our hill in its turn roar together, and the murmurs of worse rumour be silent! For he remains, and through returning ages long shall remain, the man in whose hands is the gentle guardianship of fearless Rome; nor shall the new ages clothe themselves in this crime of fate, nor shall the altar of refounded Tarentum have sinned. But I will not summon Phoebus, though without him my quills are dumb, nor the Aonian goddesses with Pallas as their tenth, nor will I urge the gentle Tegean nursling of Dirce: come yourself, and supply new strength and spirit, you of whom I sing; for not without a learned power, so great, have you given the broad honours of the Ausonian toga and a hundred men their judgement and their mind, though the inspired Pimplea shut out the poet's thirst and Pirene, the witness, be not given: rather give me a flood for ample draughts, caught from your own spring, whether you build your discourse smooth in loosened measures, or whether eloquence is bent sweetly to your art and tends our laws. Therefore come; if we render to Ceres her own gifts and to Lyaeus unmixed wine, and Diana, rich in spoil, receives the spoils of the chase upon her whole dome, and the war-god the captive weapons: nor will you—since you, Gallicus, have a greater eloquence and abound, sublime, in the wealth of speech— disdain to be honoured on a slenderer lyre. The wandering moon is girdled with stars, and lesser streams have fallen into the ocean. What rewards for your character did the City's love anxiously pay you! What lights then of fathers and knights did I mark, and of the unknowing commons mourning the powerful? Not when Numa was failing did the happy Curia so fear, nor the lofty knight for Pompey, nor the women for Brutus. This was that: to hear unwilling the sad chains, to spare the lash, and not to go where high power bids you go, but to take from yourself much of your armed force and to hold humble hands worthy and the words of suppliants, to render justice to the forum, not to overturn the curule chairs and to soften iron with the toga. So one comes into deep hearts, so reverence steals in mingled with love. The grave harshness of sudden fate too struck all men with fear, and the headlong youthful peril of a swift danger, the evil delaying nothing. That was no fault of old age— for it had scarcely begun to pass beyond its twelfth lustrum— but toil that strained, and the rule of a vigorous mind over the limbs, and the watchful cares for his Caesar, a sweet task. Hence into his weary frame crept deep an insidious quiet and a sluggish forgetting of life. Then the god who, beside the summits of the Alpine ridge, marks the Apolline groves with a holy name, looks—alas—on the nursling he had long left secure, and cutting short delay: 'Now with me, child of Epidaurus, go from here,' he says, 'go gladly: a chance is given—it must be tried— to restore a mighty man. Let us set to and lay hold of the distaff that already draws out the threads: fear not the black thunderbolt: Jupiter himself will praise these arts of his own accord. For it is no plebeian soul, nor one sprung without a favouring power, that I save—and indeed I will tell it briefly, while we go beneath his roof. His own family permitted him, and a nobility reaching back: nor is his origin hidden, but it is outdone by the light that follows, and rejoices to have yielded to so great a grandson. The toga's first virtue was his too: famous and great in eloquence; then his sworn troops, tried in countless camps, earned the houses of the West and the East and under every sun, nor was it allowed in the leisure of peace to relax their spirits and ungird the iron. Him vigorous Galatia dared to assail in war— me too—and for nine harvests Pamphylia feared him, and fierce Pannonia, and Armenia dreadful with its fleeing bow, and Araxes, now enduring the Latin bridge. Why should I unroll his twin rods and the twice-given governance of Asia? She indeed would wish to have him three and four times for her own. But the calendar recalls him, and a greater curule chair, and a promise not once made. Why should I praise the wondrous obedience of the Libyan tribute and the triumph sent from the midst of peace, and the riches so great that not even he who commissioned it dared to expect them? Trasimene rejoices, and the Alps, and the souls of Cannae; and Regulus first, with his torn shade, openly demanded the notable tribute. There is no time to tell of the Arctic lines and the rebel Rhine and the captive prayers of Veleda, and— his greatest glory of late—to throw open the City laid down to the perishing Dacians, when, chosen to take the reins of so great a ruler, Gallicus, you took them up, Fortune not wondering. This man, then—if I speak worthily—we shall snatch, my son, from unjust Jove. The famous father of the Latian city asks it, and he has deserved it; for not in vain did you, boys, lately sound honouring songs for me in your patrician purple, if there is in the healing cave of the twin Chiron any herb, whatever Trojan Pergamus stores for you in her dome or fortunate Epidaurus rears in her healing sands, the help that Idaean Crete brings forth in her shade, the strength of flowering dittany; and where the serpent abounds in his foam: I myself will join my hands, and every kindly poison that, schooled, I have plucked in the fragrant fields of Araby or from the Amphrysian grass as a shepherd.' He had spoken. They find the limbs already laid out in languor and the spirit struggling: each girds himself in the rite of Paeon, and at once they show the way and gladly obey, until with varied medicine they broke the death-bearing plagues and the suspect clouds of an evil sleep. The god himself aids the gods, and, stronger than all disease, seizes the cure; not more swiftly was Telephus restored by Haemonian art, nor those savage wounds healed with Machaon's juice that closed over the fearful son of Atreus. What place for me, among so many gatherings of people and of fathers, is there for care and prayer? Yet I call to witness the lofty stars, and you, Thymbraean father of poets—what fear was mine by every day, what by night, while, clinging to the doorposts, unceasing, now watchful with my ear, now with my eye, I catch at all— as a smaller boat, fastened to a vast ship, when the storm rages, takes in for its part of the raging sea a little water and is rolled by the same south wind. Weave now, joyful sisters, the white threads, weave! Let no one reckon the measure of the life now passed: this shall be his birthday of life. You, worthy to outstrip the Trojan ages and the years of the Euboean dust and Nestor's mouldering seat! With what poor censer now, worthy of you, can I make my plea? Not though Mevania should empty her valleys, or the fields of Clitumnus furnish snow-white bulls, should I suffice. But often, among these honours, the gods have been pleased with turf and meal from a little salt-cellar.

The Parrot of the same Parrot, prince of birds, the eloquent delight of your master, skilled imitator, parrot, of the human tongue, who has shut off your murmurs with so sudden a fate? Yesterday, poor wretch, doomed to die, you entered the feast with us, and we saw you plucking the gifts of the welcome table and wandering over the couches past the middle hour of night, and you had even given back greetings and rehearsed words. But now you hold the eternal silences of Lethe, you, that singer. Let the Phaethontian tale of the crowd give way: not the swans alone solemnize their own funerals. But what a house was yours, gleaming with russet shell, and the silver row of bars woven with ivory, and the thresholds creaking shrill at your horn, and the doors, now of their own accord complaining! That blessed prison is empty, and the chiding of the august house is nowhere! Hither let the learned birds be thronged, to whom Nature gave the noble right of speech: let the bird of Phoebus beat its breast, and the starling, mindful to send forth deep the voices it has heard, and the magpies turned in their Aonian contest, and the partridge that repeats and joins doubled words, and she who, a bereaved sister, mourns over her Bistonian bed: bring your groans together and lead the kindred funeral to the flames, and all learn this pitiable song: 'There has fallen the most renowned glory of the airy race, the parrot, green ruler of the Eastern region; whom neither the Junonian bird with its jewelled tail could outdo in look, nor the bird of cold Phasis, nor those that the Numidians snatched under the moist south wind. He, greeter of kings, who spoke the name of Caesar and once played the part of a plaintive friend, now a light table-companion, and so quick to give back the words you showed him! When you, beloved Melior, were shut in with him, you were never alone. But not unhonoured is he sent to the shades: his ashes are perfumed with Assyrian balsam and his slender plumes breathe back the grass of the Arabs and Sicanian saffron; not wearied with idle age shall the Phoenix climb the fragrant fires more happily.'
The Hair of Flavius Earinus

Go, locks, and cross, I pray, the easy sea; go, reclining softly on the crowned gold; go, gentle Cytherea will give favouring courses and will appease the south winds; perhaps even she will carry you off from the ship you fear, and lead you over the waters in her own shell. Receive the praised hair, Phoebean youth, which Caesar's boy gives to you; receive it gladly and show it to your unshorn father, let him compare the sweet gleaming locks and long think them his brother Lyaeus's. Perhaps he himself too the honour of the hair that never falls will reap and lay it for you, enclosed, in other gold. Pergamum, far happier than pine-bearing Ida! Though she please herself with the cloud of her sacred rape —surely she gave to the gods above the one whom turbulent Juno ever sees and shrinks from his hand and refuses the nectar—, yet you, dear to the gods and marked by your beautiful nursling, sent him to Latium, the minister whom with calm brow Ausonian Jupiter and Roman Juno alike look upon and both approve; nor is so great a pleasure to the powerful lord of the lands without the gods' design. It is said that, while she sought the Idalian groves from Eryx's summit and golden Venus drives her soft swans, she entered the Pergamean halls, where the greatest helper is present to the sick, and the gentle god, staying the hastening fates, broods over the health-bringing serpent. Here she catches sight of a boy, brilliant with the star of surpassing beauty, playing before the very altars of the god. And first, a little deceived by the sudden shape, she thinks him one of the children of the commons; but he had no bow and no shadows from his shining shoulders. She marvels at the boyish grace, and gazing on his face and hair, then says: 'Will you go to the Ausonian citadels, neglected by Venus? Will you bear the squalid roofs and the yoke of common servitude? Far be it: I will give to that beauty the master it has deserved. Come, go with me, go, boy: I will lead you through the stars in my winged chariot, a vast gift for the leader; nor shall plebeian rights await you: you are owed to a Palatine love. Nothing, nothing, I confess, in all the world have I seen or begotten so sweet. The Latmian shall yield to you of his own accord and the Sangarian boy, and he whom the empty image of the spring and a sterile love consumed. You the dark-blue Naiad would have preferred, and, your urn seized, would have drawn you more strongly. You, boy, before all; he alone is more beautiful, to whom you shall be given.' So beginning, she lifts him lightly with her through the air and bids him sit in her swan-drawn chariot. And no delay: now the Latian mountains and the dwellings of old Evander, which the famous father of the world adorns with new mass and makes Germanicus equal to the highest stars. Then a nearer care for the goddess: what form is best for the hair, what dress fit to kindle the rosy face, what gold more worthy on the fingers, what on the neck. She knew the heavenly eyes of the leader, and herself had joined the torches and with full hand given the marriage: so she adorns his locks, so pours the Tyrian mantle, gives the rays and her own fire. The former delights gave way and the troops of servants; he carries the first cups to the great leader, and the heavy myrrh-vessels and crystal, with a whiter hand: a new grace grows for Bacchus. Boy dear to the gods above, chosen to taste beforehand the venerable nectar and so often to touch the mighty hand, which the Getae long to know, which the Persians and Armenians and Indians long to touch! O born under a favouring star, much has the gods' indulgence smiled on you! Once too, lest the first down should pluck your shining cheeks and the grace of your beautiful form should darken, the god himself left the lofty Pergamum of his fatherland across the seas. To no one was the power to soften the boy entrusted, but the Phoebean youth, with silent art, gently bids the body, shaken by no wound, pass from its sex; yet anxious with cares Cytherea is gnawed and fears the boy's pains. Not yet had the leader's fair clemency begun, from his rising, to keep males untouched; now to break the sex and change a man is a sin, and rejoicing nature sees only those whom she begot, nor by a sinister law do the slave-mothers fear to bear the burdens of their sons. You too now, a young man, had you been born later, your cheeks shaded and stronger in your grown limbs, would have sent no single gift, rejoicing, to the Phoebean threshold; but now your hair alone sails to your father's shores. This with much balsam the Paphian was saturating, this the new Grace combed with her threefold hand; to this the wounded hair of purple Nisus yields, and that which swelling Achilles kept for the Spercheus. To the boy himself, when first it was resolved to crop his snowy brow and bare his shining shoulders with the hand, there come the tender winged ones with the Paphian mother and free his locks and lay the Seric mantle from his breast; then with joined arrows they cut the hair and set it in gold and gems; his mother herself snatches the falling locks and Cytherea repeats the secret liquids. Then a boy from the throng, who chanced with upturned hands to have carried a noble mirror of jewelled gold, 'Let us give this too,' he says; 'no gift will be more welcome to your father's temples, and more powerful than the gold itself. Only fix your gaze and leave your face here forever.' So he speaks and unlocked the mirror, its image seized. But the excellent boy, stretching his palms to the stars, 'For these gifts, gentlest keeper of men, if I have deserved it, may you renew my lord with long youth and keep him for the world! This the stars with me, this the waters and lands ask: let him go, I pray, through the years of Ilium and Pylos alike, and rejoice in his own home and let the Tarpeian temples grow old with him.' So he speaks, and Pergamum marvels at the moved altars.
A Letter to Vitorius Marcellus Run, letter, not sluggish, through the Euboean fields,
setting out by this way, where the noble Appian rises
on its flank and the solid causeway presses the soft sands.
And when you have swiftly entered the towers of Romulus,
at once make for the right bank of the tawny Tiber,
where the Lydian shore shuts in the naval pool deep within
and the channel is fringed with suburban gardens;
there you will see Marcellus, distinguished in beauty and in spirit,
and you will know him, conspicuous by his lofty head.
To him first give the common people's customary greeting,
then remember to render these words shaped in verse:
'Now the flight of the watery spring loosens the lands
and the swift sky, and burns the heaven with the Icarian dog-star;
now the steep walls of crowded Rome grow thin;
sacred Praeneste shelters these men, the icy grove of Diana those,
Algidus either bristling or the Tusculan shade,
these seek the groves of Tibur and the cool of the Anio.
You too—what gentler region withdraws you
from the clamorous city? With what air do you cheat the summer suns?
And what of Gallus, before all others your chief care,
and our love too—doubtful whether to be approved for goodness
of character or of talent—does he take the summer on Latian shores,
or does he seek again the walls of metal-bearing Luna
