and the Tyrrhenian houses? But if he keeps close to you,
then I am not now far from your conversation;
it is certain: from there the sound circles about my two ears.
But you, while the grim mane of the Cleonaean star
blazes, possessed by Hyperion too near, strip your breast
of cares and steal yourself away from constant toil.
The Parthian too covers his guilty quivers and unstrings his bow,
and the Elean charioteer soothes in the Alpheus
the horses driven by his labours; and our lyre
grows weary and is loosed: timely rest
stirs and feeds our strength; greater is virtue after leisure!
Such, when Briseis had been sung, did Achilles come
keener, and, laying down his quill, broke out against Hector.
You too will kindle the more for a little while of idleness
silently resumed, and renewed will leap into your wonted deeds.
Certainly now the Latian laws do not stir up quarrels,
and the slow year holds peace, and the returning harvests
have dismissed the Forum; nor now does the crowd of defendants
throng your porch, nor do querulous clients ask you to come out;
the spear that governs the court of a hundred judges is at rest,
the spear by which you already stand most renowned
in lofty fame, and your young eloquence outstrips your years.
Happy in your cares, you who care nothing for Heliconian
garlands nor the unwarlike laurels from Parnassus's height,
but your genius thrives, and girt up for great employments
your spirit bears whatever changes come: we comfort the leisure
of our life with song, and seek the windy joys of fame.
Behold, I myself, following sleep and the genial shore
where Parthenope the stranger hid herself in an Ausonian port,
strike the slender strings with idle thumb,
and sitting on the margin of Maro's temple
take up my spirit and sing in answer to the swelling strains of the great master:
but you, if Atropos shall grant the course of a long life
—and may she grant it, I pray, and so may the powers of the Latian leader prosper,
whom you have made it your zeal to worship, setting even the Thunderer second,
and who has woven into your office another duty
and bids you renew the spaces of the winding Latin Way!—
perhaps you will go to bridle the Ausonian cohorts,
or the peoples of the Rhine, or the shores of black Thule,
or it will be given you to guard the Hister and the dreaded
thresholds of the Caspian gate. For not yours alone is the virtue
of powerful eloquence: you have limbs fitted for wars
and arms that would slowly take up the heavy breastplate:
whether you should go on foot in the field, above the lines
a nodding crest will tower; or you will turn the sounding reins,
the rough horse will serve you. We, singing the deeds of others,
decline toward old age: you, beautiful in your own arms,
will yourself do deeds worth singing, and small Geta
you will furnish with great examples, whom even now his warlike
grandfather demands for warlike deeds, and grants him to know triumphs at home.
Rise, come, boy, take after the young man your father,
happy in your mother's lineage, in your father's virtue.
Now in her Tyrian lap fair Gloria gladly
rears you for herself, and rejoices to promise all the curule chairs.'
This I was sounding to you, Marcellus, from the Chalcidian
shores, where Vesuvius lifts its broken rage,
rolling fires that rival the flames of Trinacria.
A wonder hard to believe! Will future generations believe
that, when crops grow again, when this waste land grows green,
cities and peoples lie pressed below, and ancestral
fields have passed away by a like fate? Nor does the deadly
peak yet cease to threaten. Far from your Teate be that doom,
nor let this madness drive the Marrucinian mountains.
Now if perchance you ask what the beginnings of my Muse may be,
now, having measured the Sidonian labours, my Thebaid
has gathered its sails in the longed-for harbour
and on the ridges of Parnassus and the Heliconian wood
has given incense to the festal flames and the entrails of a virgin heifer,
and hung up my fillets on the vow-bearing tree.
Now another fillet binds my empty hair with a new knot:
Troy indeed and great Achilles I attempt,
but the Archer-father calls me elsewhere and shows me arms
greater, those of the Ausonian leader; impulse draws me there
already and long since, and fear draws me back: will my shoulders
stand beneath that mass, or will my neck be conquered by the great weight?
Tell me, Marcellus, shall I bear it? Or shall a ship
used to know smaller waves not yet be trusted to Ionian perils?
And now farewell, and forbid the honour of your vows for the bard
deeply to leave your heart; for the Tirynthian was not
the parent of kindly friendship: to you shall yield the glory of faithful
Theseus, and of him who dragged the mangled son of Priam
round the walls of Troy for solace, his comrade slain.
Sleep By what crime have I deserved, gentlest youth of the gods,
or by what error, wretched, that I alone should lack
your gifts, Sleep? Every herd is silent, the birds and the beasts,
and the curved tree-tops feign weary slumbers,
nor have the fierce rivers the same sound; the shudder of the sea
dies down, and the seas, leaning on the lands, grow quiet.
Now the seventh returning moon looks back on my sick
eyes still standing open; as many times the Oetaean and Paphian
torches revisit me, and as often Tithonia passes by
my complaints and, pitying, sprinkles me with her cold whip.
Whence shall I find strength? Not if I had the thousand eyes
which sacred Argus kept only in alternating watch,
and never kept awake with his whole body.
But now, alas! if someone through the long night, holding
a girl's arms entwined, drives you off of his own will, Sleep,
from there come; nor do I bid you pour all your wings
over my eyes—let the happier throng pray for that—:
touch me with the very tip of your wand,
it is enough, or pass lightly over with hovering knee.

The Bath of Claudius Etruscus My inspired lyre does not beat Helicon with a heavy quill, nor do I call the Muses, the powers so often wearied for me; and you, Phoebus, and you, Euhan, I dismiss from the choir. You too, winged Tegean, lay your back, dumb, upon the sounding beast: my songs ask for other companies. The Naiads, mistresses of the waters, and the king of the gleaming fire, still weary and glowing from the Sicilian anvil, it is enough to have drawn forth. Lay aside a little your harmful arms, Thebes: I wish to be playful for a beloved comrade. Pour the cups, boy—but do not labour to count them— and tighten the lingering lyre: depart, Toil and Care, while I sing the baths that gleam with bright gems and, my Clio wanton with fillets and ivy, her modest leaves loosed, plays for Etruscus. Go, green goddesses, and turn hither your liquid faces and crown your glassy hair with tender clusters, clothed in no garment, as you rise from the deep fountains and torment the loving Satyrs with the sight— not you who by your fault have shamed the glory of the waters do I wish to summon: far from here let Salmacis go, and the streams of the widowed daughter of Cebren, dry with grief, and the ravisher of the Herculean nursling. You, nymphs, who dwell in Latium and the seven peaks and lift up the Tiber with new waters, whom headlong Anio, and the Virgin who receives the swimmer, delight, and Marcia who draws the Marsian snows and frosts, whose wandering wave grows upon lofty masses and, hanging, is carried across on countless arches— your work I undertake; yours is the house I unfold in soft song, nor have you ever dwelt more richly in other caves. Cytherea herself held her husband's hand and showed his arts: lest cheap blasts should scorch the furnaces, she herself kindled the torches of the winged Loves. No Thasos was admitted here, nor wave-washed Carystos; onyx mourns far off, and the serpentine, shut out, complains: the purple alone gleams, cut from the tawny mines of the Numidians, and that alone which Phrygian Synnas, in its hollow cave, Attis himself stained with bright spots, and the snowy rocks that Tyre and Sidon cut, where there is scarcely room for the Eurotas, when the green vein varies Synnas with its long pattern; the thresholds do not fail, the vaults blaze, and the gables with varied glass shine into shapes and spirits. The fire itself is amazed, embracing the blessed wealth, and rules more sparingly. Much daylight everywhere, where the sun pierces the roofs with all its rays and burns with another's heat. Nothing plebeian there: nowhere will you mark Temesan bronze. But the water flows happily, driven by silver, and falls by silver and presses upon the shining basins, marvelling at its own delights and refusing to leave. But outside, the dark-blue stream that lives within its snowy margin, all open from the depth to the surface from below, whom would it not urge to go into the pool and loose his sluggish garments? Cytherea would have wished to be born in this deep. Here you would have seen yourself more clearly, Narcissus; here swift Hecate would wish, and, caught, to bathe. Why should I now tell of the floors laid upon the ground, that will hear the rattling balls, where the languid fire wanders through the chambers and the hypocausts roll their thin steam? Nor, should a new guest come from the Baian shores, would he scorn such things—let it be allowed to set small beside great—nor would he who has just bathed in the Neronian wave refuse to sweat here again. A blessing, I pray, on your shining genius and care, boy! May these grow old with you, and may your fortune now learn better to be reborn!

The Tame Lion What did it profit you now to grow tame, your rage laid low? What to unlearn in your spirit the wickedness and the human slaughters, and to suffer command and obey a lesser master? What of this—that you were wont to go from home and return again to your cage, and now of your own accord to withdraw from the captured prey and to let go the inserted hands with a slackened bite? You fall, learned ravager of tall wild beasts, not shut in by the Massylian band or the curving net, nor driven on, in your dreaded leap above the hunting-spears, nor cheated by the blind gape of the pit, but conquered by a fleeing beast. The unlucky cage stands with its hinge open, and around the gates shut on every side the gentle lions swelled that such a crime was allowed; then all their manes drooped, and they were ashamed to look back at the report, and drew their whole brows down over their eyes. But you, laid low at the first blow, that new shame did not overwhelm: your spirit remained, and valour returns to you as you fall, even from the midst of death; nor at once did all your threats turn tail, but, like a soldier conscious of a deep wound, who, dying, goes against the foe and lifts his hand and threatens with the sword that slips away: so you, sluggish in your tread and stripped of your wonted honour, fix your gaping eyes and seek both your life and your foe. Yet great solace of your sudden death you bear with you, vanquished one: that the people and the fathers grieved your dying, as though you fell, a known gladiator on the sad sand; that, amid so many Scythian and Libyan beasts, and from the shore of Rhine and of the Egyptian race—beasts it is cheap to lose— the loss of one lion touched great Caesar's face.

Eclogue to his Wife Why so sad, tell me, why through the shared nights, wife, anxious and sleepless, do you draw out sighs of care? I do not fear that your faith is broken or that in that heart is another love; against you no arrows are allowed to go —let the Rhamnusian hear it with hostile face—it is not allowed, and even if I myself, snatched from my native shore, through wars, through seas for four full lustres, should wander, you would put a thousand suitors to flight, untouched, not feigning to unweave the cut threads, but openly, without deceit, you would have refused the bridal chamber, armed. Yet tell me, whence this lofty brow and clouded face? Is it because, weary, I divine that I shall return to my Euboean home and lay my old age to rest in my native land? Why is this sad to you? Surely no wantonness is in your heart, nor do the swift battles of the Circus soothe you, nor does the crowd of the clamorous theatre enter your senses; but honesty and shaded quiet and joys never base. But to what waves do I snatch you as my comrade? And yet, even if I were going to dwell beside the cold Bears, or above the darkening shoals of Hesperian Thule, or to the impenetrable head of the sevenfold Nile, you would urge my ways. For yours—surely with kindly lot Venus keeps you joined to me in my flowering years and into old age—yours, who pierced me with my first wound untouched by the bridal chamber and still wandering in my youth, your reins, gladly and teachably I received, and the bridle once set in I shall never change but ever press; you, when I bore the Alban gifts in my bright hair and was holily clad in Caesar's gold, embracing me to your heart, with garlands gave panting kisses to mine; you, when the Capitol denied my lyre, grieved with me, conquered, over savage and ungrateful Jove; you snatch with wakeful ear my songs running forward at their first sounds, and whole nights in their murmur; you alone, the witness of my long labour, and as my Thebaid grew with your years, such as I lately saw you, when I was snatched near the Stygian shades, when I was hearing the Lethean streams close at hand, and held my eyes already falling in death; surely Lachesis, the times of my exhausted fate now spent, pitying you alone, gave them back, and the powerful gods above feared your envy. After all this, do you, my comrade, delay to go on the near journey now and to the longed-for bays? Alas, where is the known faith, tested through so many uses, by which you match the old heroines of Latium and Greece? To the Ilian halls Penelope would have gone, rejoicing— for why should she let her lovers keep her?—had Ulysses suffered it; Aegiale complained, Meliboea complained, of being left, and she whom—how savage they were!—her beatings made a maenad. No less than these are you. To know one faith and to give your life to your husbands—so surely you still seek the ashes and the former shade, so, embracing the obsequies of your tuneful husband, you repeated the great beatings in your breast, now mine. Nor is your devotion other, nor your care for your daughter; so too as a mother you love, so never from your heart does your daughter depart, and fixed in your soul's inmost shrines you hold her night and day. Not so does the Trachinian Alcyone circle her nests, not so does Philomela her spring dwellings, embracing, and pour her soul into her young. Now she holds you, because in a widowed bed alone she now wears away the barren leisure of her lovely youth. But they will come, the weddings will come with full torches. So surely she deserves by the gifts of beauty and mind; whether, embracing the lyre, she seeks it, or with her father's voice sounds what must be learned by the Muses and shapes my songs, or whether she parts her white arms in soft motion: her honesty conquers her genius, her modesty her art. Will not the light boys, will not you, Cytherea, be ashamed that this beauty lies idle? Nor is Rome alone fertile to reconcile the wedded couches and kindle the festive torches: in our land too sons-in-law shall be given. Not so far did the Vesuvian peak and the fiery storm of the dread mountain drain the trembling cities of their citizens: they stand and flourish with peoples; here, founded under Phoebus's auspices, the houses of Dicarchus, and the harbour and shores hospitable to the world; but here the tracts that imitate great Rome, the walls that Capys filled with the Teucrians he brought, ours too, and not rare with its own slender colonists, Parthenope, to whom Apollo himself showed the gentle soil across the seas with a Dionaean dove. These seats I labour to bring you to—for neither is barbarous Thrace nor Libya my native soil—, seats which soft winter and cool summer temper, which the unwarlike sea washes with sluggish waves, where there is secure peace in the places, and the leisure of an idle life, and quiet never disturbed, and slumbers fully slept. No fury in the forum, nor laws drawn for quarrels: the only law for men is the law of character, and justice without rods. Why now should I tell of the magnificent sights and the adornments of the places, the temples and the spaces set off by countless columns, and the twin mass of the open and roofed theatre, and the five-yearly games next to the Capitoline rites, why should I praise the shore and the freedom of Menander, which Roman dignity and Greek licence mingle? Nor are there wanting various delights round about life: whether the most coaxing shores, Baiae with their steam, or to visit the inspired roofs of the prophetic Sibyl be sweet, and the ridge memorable for the Ilian oar, or whether the dripping vineyards of Bacchic Gaurus and the homes of the Teleboae please you, where for trembling sailors the Pharos lifts its sweet lights, rival of the night-wandering moon, and the dear Surrentine ridges not poor in soft Lyaeus, which my own dweller, Pollius, before all others enriches, and the healing lakes of Aenaria and Stabiae reborn: shall I recount to you a thousand loves of our land? But enough; this, wife, it is enough to have said: it created me for you, it bound me as your comrade for the long years. Is not this land worthy to be seen as the mother and nurse of us both? But I am ungrateful, who add more and doubt your character: you will come, dearest wife, and will even come before me; without me Tiber the lord of waters and the roofs of arms-bearing Quirinus shall seem mean to you.

pr. Statius to his friend Marcellus, greeting. I have found a book, dearest Marcellus, to dedicate to your devotion. For my part I think no little work of mine ought to begin otherwise than by invoking the godhead of our greatest emperor: but this book has three . . . than the fourth, which belongs to your honour. In the first I paid homage to the seventeenth consulship of our Germanicus; in the second I gave thanks, honoured by being his guest at that most sacred banquet; in the third I marvelled at the Domitian Way, by which he removed the heaviest obstacle of the sands. By its gift you too will receive my letter the sooner, the letter I write to you in this book from Naples. Next comes the lyric poem to Septimius Severus, a young man, as you know, among the most distinguished of the second rank, your friend and fellow-pupil, but dear to me most closely even apart from this claim. As for the Hercules Epitrapezios of our Vindex, I can charge it to your account as the second tribute owed to me and to these studies themselves. That I esteem Vibius Maximus for his rank and his eloquence I had testified well enough in the letter I published to him about the publication of my Thebaid; but now too I beg him to return the sooner from Dalmatia. Joined to these is an eclogue to my fellow-townsman Julius Menecrates, a splendid young man and the son-in-law of my friend Pollius, whom I congratulate on having honoured our Naples with the number of his children. To Plotius Grypus, a young man of higher standing, I shall render a worthier little work, but in the meantime I have inserted into this volume the hendecasyllables over which we laughed together at the Saturnalia. Why then more in the fourth book of Silvae than in the earlier ones? So that those who have found fault—as I hear—because I published this kind of writing may not think they have achieved anything. First, it is useless to dissuade from a thing already done; next, I had already given many of these poems to my lord Caesar—and how much more is that than publishing? And is one not permitted to amuse oneself in jest? In private, he says. But we watch sham fights too, and the sport of fencing admits spectators. Lastly: whoever reads anything of mine against his will at once declares himself my enemy. So why should I defer to his judgement? In sum, it is surely I who am being put on trial; let him hold his peace and rejoice. This book, however, you, Marcellus, will defend; and if it seems good, so far; if not, I shall be reproached. Farewell.
A Lyric Ode to Septimius Severus Blessed in the honours of a little farm,
where ancient Alba tends its Teucrian household gods,
I salute brave and eloquent Severus
with strings not customary.
Already the fierce winter to the Parrhasian Bears
has withdrawn, overwhelmed by lofty suns;
already sea and land shine bright
toward the Zephyrs, the North Wind broken.
Now with the spring's yearly leaves the tree
grows leafy-haired, now the birds' new
complaints and untried song,
which they fixed in the silent winter.
A frugal earth and a watchful hearth and a roof
grimy with much firelight console us,
and the wine drawn from the jar
in which but now Lyaeus had simmered.
A thousand wool-bearing flocks do not bleat,
no cow lows for her sweet mate,
and if ever to one man singing
the mute field cries back its lord alone.
But this land is dear to me, after my homeland, with my first
cares: here my songs the warrior queen,
the maiden of wars,
loved well, with Caesar's gold,
when you, the sweet peril of your comrade,
striving with all your heart, would lift him up,
as Castor trembled at every
uproar of the Bebrycian sand.
Did remote Leptis, in the trackless Syrtes,
create you? Soon she will bear Indian
harvests, and snatch the rare cinnamon
before the fragrant Sabaeans.
Who would not think that on every height of Romulus
sweet Septimius had crawled as a child?
Who would deny that at the fount of Juturna,
the breasts forsaken, he was nourished?
No wonder your virtue: at once you entered the harbours
of the Ausonians, ignorant of shallow Africa,
and adopted by the Tuscan
streams, as a boy you swam.
Hence, small among the children of the senate-house,
content with the light of the narrow purple,
you grew, but pursued immense labours
with patrician character.
No Punic speech, no Punic dress was yours,
no foreign mind: an Italian, an Italian!
There are in the City and the Roman squadrons
foster-sons who would do honour to Libya.
You have a cheerful voice in the roaring Forum,
but your eloquence is not for sale;
your sword rests in its sheath,
unless your friends bid you draw it.
But the country is dearer to you, and quiet, more often,
now in your father's seat and on Veientine
soil, now above the leafy
Hernican hills, now at ancient Cures.
Here you will set down more in voices and in measures
with loosened step, but mindful meanwhile
of me, redouble the lyre that lies hidden
modestly beneath your cave.
A Funeral Lament for His Boy Wretched me! For with no solemn words shall I
begin now, hateful to the vocal waves of Castalia
and grievous to Phoebus. What rites of yours, sisters,
Pierian, what altars have I defiled?
Tell me; after the punishment, let me confess what I have committed.
Have I set my footsteps in some forbidden grove?
Have I drunk from a forbidden fount? What fault, what error
so great do I expiate? Behold, with dying arms
clasping my entrails, the infant is torn away, and his soul;
not of my stock indeed, nor one to bear my name
and face; I was not his father—but see my tears
and livid cheeks, and believe in the lamentations of the bereaved:
I am bereaved. Hither let fathers and mothers with open breast
assemble; and bring his ashes to your eyes, and your crimes,
if any woman has, beneath full breasts, to a funeral
borne her own children, herself with sinking step, and let her wet
breast fall and quench with milk the burning embers.
Whoever has plunged into the ashes a youth marked
with the flower of tender youth, and has seen the cruel flames
creep with the first down over him as he lies,
let him be present and grow weary with me in alternate cry:
he will be overcome by tears, and you, Nature, will be ashamed.
So great is my fierceness, so great the madness of my grief,
that even this, when I strive, the thirtieth daylight passed,
leaning on the tomb, and turn lamentation into songs,
and labour at discordant measures and sobbing words:
the lyre's force, and a wrath impatient of silence,
begins. But neither the wonted laurel on my head
nor the filleted honour on my brow; behold, the yew
withers in my hair, and the bewept cypress shuts out
the glad ivy with its branches; nor with ivory thumb
do I strike the strings, but with wandering fingers, frantic,
I tear the uncertain lyre. It pleases, alas, it pleases to pour out
an unpraised song and rudely to lay bare my wretched grief.
Have I deserved this? So in song and garb accursed
let the gods above behold me? Let them be ashamed of Thebes and the new
Aeacid? Will nothing peaceful now flow from my lips?
I who—how often!—could fondly soften the wounds of mothers
and fathers, who could soothe widowed griefs,
I, the gentle consoler of mourners, heard
at bitter tombs and by the descending shades,
I fail, and seek for helping hands and remedies
for my wounds, but the worst, my own. Now is the time, friends,
whose streaming eyes and wounded breasts I have wiped:
render aid, pay your cruel thanks.
Doubtless, when I reproached your funerals with sad measures:
'you who grieve for another's losses, lay by,
unhappy man, your tears and keep your sorrowful songs.'
It was true: my strength is spent and no abundance of speech
is mine, and my mind has found nothing worthy of so great a thunderbolt:
every voice is inferior and all words are mean.
Pardon, boy: you overwhelm me with sad gloom.
Ah! hard would he be who, the wound of his dear wife seen,
found something for Thracian Orpheus to sing sweet
to himself, who, if Apollo, embracing the pyre of Linus,
was not silent—am I perhaps called too much and too greedy of grief,
and to have exceeded in tears a just modesty?
But who reproaches my groans and laments?
O too happy, too cruel, and free
of your sway, Fortune, is he who dares to dictate a law
to weeping or to assess the bounds of grieving!
It urges, alas, the wailing: sooner might you stay rivers
fleeing their banks, or stand against swift fires,
than forbid the wretched to mourn. Yet let that stern one,
whoever he is, learn the wounds of my cause.
I did not love a chattering darling bought from a Pharian ship,
a child taught the railleries of his own Nile,
too forward of tongue and in his wit; he was mine, mine.
I saw him falling to earth, and anointed with the natal song
I cherished him, and as he begged with trembling cries
new airs, I inserted him into life. What more do parents give?
Indeed I gave you another birth and freedom under your very
breasts, little one, when you laughed at our gifts,
ungrateful as yet—and he made haste,
but rightly he made haste, my love, lest your freedom,
so small, should lose a single day. Shall I not then, grim
with envy, beat the gods above and unjust Tartarus?
Shall I not bewail you, dear boy? You whose safety I desired
more than sons; whom, begotten, at his very first dawn
I clasped and fixed to myself; to whom I showed words
and sounds, and unbound his hidden complaints and wounds,
and as he crawled on the ground, stooping to our kisses,
I raised him up, and in my caressing lap, again and again
as they sank, lulled his eyelids to rest and summoned sweet sleep.
His first voice held my name, and his play
was my laughter, and from my face came his joys.

The Kalends of December Both Phoebus our father and stern Pallas and the Muses, go far off and take your holiday: on the Kalends of Janus we will recall you. Saturn, his fetter undone, and December heavy with much wine, and laughing Jest and the saucy Witticisms, be present with me, while I tell of the blessed day of the glad Caesar and the merry foretaste of the year. Scarce was the Dawn stirring her new risings, when already sweets were raining in a line —this dew the rising east wind poured forth: whatever noble fruit the Pontic nut-groves bear, or falls from the fruitful ridges of Idyme; what pious Damascus brings forth on its boughs, and what drunken Caunus ripens to the full, came down for nothing in lavish plunder: soft cakes and little dumplings, and Amerine fruits not scorched in their lumps, and must-cake, and date-palm clusters, swollen and pregnant, were falling. Not with such showers does the unclear Hyas overwhelm the lands, nor the loosed Pleiades, as the storm pounded the people through the Latin rows with hail from a cloudless sky. Let Jupiter lead his clouds across the world and threaten the broad fields with rain, so long as these showers of our Jove are borne. But lo, through all the seats there enters a folk remarkable in look, comely in dress, another people, no less than the seated one. These carry baskets and white napkins and richer fare; those lavish mellow wines: you would think them so many Idaean cupbearers. The world, in its better and sterner part, and the nations clad in togas you feed at once; and since you nourish so many peoples, blessed one, proud Annona knows nothing of this day. Go now, Antiquity, compare the ages, the time of ancient Jove and the age of gold: not so freely did the wine then flow, nor did the harvest take the laggard year; at one table every rank feasts, children, women, commons, knights, the senate: freedom has relaxed its reverence. And you yourself too—who of the gods could promise this, or have leisure for it?— have entered into the shared feast with us. Now each man, whoever he is, poor or rich, glories that he is the guest of our leader. Amid these uproars and new delights the light pleasure of watching slips away: there stands a sex untrained and ignorant of the sword; how the shameless thing takes up manly battles! You would think the Thermodontian squadrons were heating to war by Tanais and fierce Phasis. Here advances a bold rank of dwarfs, whom nature, briefly finished at once, bound forever into a knotted ball; they deal wounds and join their hands and threaten themselves with death—by what a hand! Father Mars laughs, and bloody Valour, and the cranes, about to fall to wandering plunder, marvel that the boxers are fiercer than they. Now, under the nearer shadows of night, what tumults does the rich largess set astir! Here enter girls easily to be bought, here is recognized all that wins approval in the theatres for beauty or for art. Here the plump Lydian women clap their troops, there cymbals and tinkling Gades, there the bands of Syrians roar together, here the stage-folk and those who barter common sulphur for broken glass. Amid all this, in sudden flight, there fall through the stars immense clouds of birds, which sacred Nile and dreadful Phasis, which the Numidians gather under the moist south wind: there are not enough to seize them, and full bosoms rejoice as new spoils are won. They raise to the stars their countless voices, sounding the Saturnalia of the prince, and with sweet favour acclaim their lord: this alone Caesar forbade to be allowed. Scarce was the dark-blue night entering the world, when down into the midst of the bright arena descended a flaming globe amid the thick shadows, outshining the torch of the Cnossian crown; the sky blazes with fires, and lets nothing be permitted to the dark night, sluggish Quiet flees, and idle Sleep seeing this departs to other cities. Who shall sing the shows, who the licensed jests, who the banquets, who the unbought feasts, who the streams of lavish Lyaeus? Now, now I faint, and by your Bacchus am drawn, drunk, into late slumber. Through how many years far off shall this day go, and by no age shall its sacred memory fade! While the Latian hills and father Tiber endure, while your Rome shall stand, and while the Capitol that you restore to the lands shall remain.
pr. Statius to his Melior, greeting.

Both our intimacy, in which I rejoice, Melior—best of men, and as flawless in your judgement of letters as in every shade of your life—and the very nature of the little works I hand over to you are so disposed that this whole book of mine looks to you even without a letter. For first it contains our Glaucias, whose most charming infancy (such as the unlucky generally draw by lot) I loved in your embrace—now no longer yours. The wound of his recent loss, as you know, I followed with a funeral elegy so hastily that I have had to excuse my speed to your own feelings. Nor do I now boast of it to you, who know it, but I declare it to the rest, lest anyone weigh the poem with too harsh a file: it was written with confidence and given to one in grief, when slow consolations are almost superfluous. The Surrentine villa of my Pollius, which follows, I ought to have rendered more carefully, if only in honour of his eloquence; but my friend has pardoned me. As for your tree, Melior, and the parrot, you know that I wrote these slight little pieces as if in place of epigrams. The same ease of style was required by the tame lion, which, laid low in the amphitheatre, it would have been frigid not to hand at once to our most sacred Emperor. To our Ursus too, a most candid young man and most learned without any loss to his diligence, I have gladly inserted in this book a consolation written on the loss of his favourite boy, over and above what I owe to himself, because his honour will be set to your credit when I bear it to you. A birthday poem for Lucan closes the volume, which Polla Argentaria, rarest of wives, when we chanced to consult about this day, wished to be charged to her account. I could show no greater reverence for so great an author than this—that, intending to speak his praises, I feared my own hexameters. These pieces, such as they are, dearest Melior: if they have not displeased you, let them receive their publication from you; if not, let them return to me.

Consolation to Flavius Ursus on the loss of his favourite boy Too cruel, whoever sets limits to tears and measures to mourning. It is wretched for a parent to kindle—unspeakable!—the pyre of his firstborn pledges and his rising sons; hard, too, to bewail the loss of a bedfellow snatched away, the empty half of the couch, and the sad laments of sisters and the groans of brothers: yet deep and far within it enters more deeply into the senses, and conquers with greater wounds, the lesser blow—a slave (because Fortune with blind hand so confounds the names of things and knows not the heart)— but a slave, Ursus, you mourn, a faithful one, who by love and loyalty earned these tears, who had a freedom greater than any joined lineage, springing from his mind. Do not press down your weeping, do not be ashamed; let that grief break its reins, and the daylight, if such hard things please—you mourn a man—alas! I myself set the torches—a man, Ursus, your own, to whom servitude was sweet when he willed it, to whom nothing was sad, who of his own accord and over himself was commanding. Who would chastise the mourning sent out for such a death? The Parthian groans for his horse killed in war, the Molossians wept their faithful dogs, and birds have had their pyre, and the stag wept for Maro. What if he were not even a slave? I myself saw, and marked your looks, desiring you only as master; but greater was the spirit in his face, and his character plainly shown in his tender blood. Greek and Latin daughters-in-law would much have wished and longed to have borne such a son; not such did the cunning Cretan recall proud Theseus with her anxious thread, nor did Paris, rustic, about to behold the Oebalian love, launch the unwilling pines into the sea. I do not deceive, nor does the licence wonted to song lead me on: I saw, and still see, such as Thetis hid, singing no war, on the virgin shore, her Achilles, nor such as the Haemonian spear of the right hand caught, Troilus, fleeing around the walls of savage Phoebus. What you were! Behold, far fairer than all boys and men, and only less than your master! His was the one foremost grace, as much as the bright moon outshines the lesser torches, and as much as Hesperus presses down the other fires. No womanish charm was on your face, nor above your mouth a soft grace, such as bid forms of doubtful, blemished kind pass from their sex; but a manly grace, with grim sweetness; nor was your gaze wanton, nor your eyes coaxing with a stern fire, such as, lovely already with his helmet, to the sight Parthenopaeus was; and your hair, simple with comely roughness, and your cheeks not yet beset, gleaming with their first flower: such youth does Eurotas rear in the Ledaean stream, so, untouched in his tender years, does the boy come to Elis and prove his first years to Jove. For whence such modesty in a young mind, and the tranquil moderation of your ways, and a spirit riper than your tender age, with what song could I tell again? Often he chastised you when you willed, and helped you with his zeal and deep counsels; with you sad and glad, and never his own; and he took his look from your face: worthy to surpass even Haemonian Pylades in fame and the Cecropian faith; but let there be a limit to praise, such as fortune allows: with no sounder mind, in his sickness, did Eumaeus hope for the late returns of Ulysses. What god or what chance chooses such sad wounds? Whence such a sure hand for the Fates to harm with? O how, stripped of riches and wealth, would you, Ursus, be stronger in your name! If even Vesuvian fires, smoking in ruin, had belched forth their rich Locri, or the rivers had drowned the Pollentine pastures, or Lucanian Acir, or the rush of Tiber had twisted its deep waters to the right, you would have borne the gods with serene brow; or if kindly Crete and Cyrene had denied their faith and harvests, and wherever from her happy bosom lavish Fortune comes back to you. But, knowing griefs, unhappy Envy saw the vitals of your mind and the ways of wounding. He, just at the threshold of his grown life, the fairest of youths, was trying to weave one three-year span with three Olympiads of five, when the grim Rhamnusian goddess marked him with savage face, and first filled out his frame and added a brightness to his eyes and raised his face more loftily than its wont, alas, fawning fatally on the wretch. And, looking at him, she tormented herself with envy, and, embracing his death, threw her noose upon him as he lay, and, pitiless, plucked his honoured face with curved hand. Scarce at his fifth rising did Phosphorus drive his dewy horse, when already you saw the savage shores of the hard old man, Philetus, and hard Acheron. With what cry the master called you! Not more savagely with her beating would your mother, had she lived, have blackened her dark arms for you, nor your father; and surely the brother who saw the funeral blushed to be outdone. But the fire was not servile to the lost one: the flame drank up the fragrant Sabaeans and the harvests of the Cilicians, and the cinnamon taken from the Egyptian bird, and the juices flowing from Assyrian grass, and the master's tears: these alone the embers drank, these the pyre drank to the end; nor that Setia quenched your white ashes, nor that the slippery onyx walled your bones within its bosom, was more welcome to the wretched shade than the groans—but does even that please? Why do we turn our back on grief, Ursus? Why do you cherish your loss and with an unjust heart love the wound? Where is the eloquence famed for snatched defendants? Why do you torment the dear shade with such savage mournings? Though he was excellent in spirit and deserved to be grieved: you have paid the debt; he goes to the pious and plucks the quiet of Elysium, and there perhaps has found his famous parents; or for him through the pleasant silences of Lethe perhaps the Avernal Naiads, all mingled, play on every side, and Proserpina marks him with a sidelong glance. Lay aside, I pray, your laments; the Fates will give you another Philetus, and perhaps he himself will give one, and will gladly show you comely ways and bearing, and teach you a like love.
The Hercules Epitrapezios of Novius Vindex By chance, as I was easing my cares and lightening
my breast of Phoebus, wandering at leisure through the open Saepta
with the day now dying, the supper of kindly
Vindex carried me off; and this, having glided into the deep recesses of my mind,
remains unconsumed; for we did not drink in the mockeries of the belly,
nor feasts sought from the far ends of the sun,
nor wines vying with the perpetual calendar in age—
ah, wretched are they who delight to know how the bird of Phasis
differs from the wintry crane of Rhodope, which goose
bears the richer liver, why the Tuscan boar is nobler than the Umbrian,
on what seaweed the slippery shellfish may more softly recline:
ours was true love, and talk sought from the midst of Helicon,
and merry jests, that persuaded us to spend the wintry night
and to drive soft sleep from our eyes,
until from the Elysian seats the other Castor
looked forth, and Tithonia laughed at our tables of yesterday.
O good night, and would it had been joined to the Tirynthian moon!
night to be marked with the Erythraean stones of Thetis,
long to be remembered, and to have a lasting genius!
A thousand kinds of bronze and ancient ivory there
and waxen figures that seem to speak with their mimic bodies
I learned by heart. For who anywhere could rival with his eyes
Vindex, in recognizing the old strokes of the craftsmen
and giving the maker back to unsigned statues?
He will show you what bronzes much-vigilant skill wrought for learned Myron,
what marbles live by the chisel of toiling
Praxiteles, what ivory was smoothed by the Pisaean thumb,
what was bidden to breathe at Polyclitus's forges,
what line proclaims old Apelles from afar:
for these things, whenever he lays aside the lyre, are his
idleness; here love calls him away to the Aonian caves.
Among these the genius and guardian of the chaste table,
the son of Amphitryon, took my breast with much love
and did not sate my eyes with long looking:
so great the honour of the work, and the majesty enclosed
within narrow bounds! A god he is, a god! and gave himself
to be seen by you, Lysippus, both seeming small
and felt to be vast! and though within a wondrous foot's
measure he stands, yet it will please you to cry out,
if you carry your gaze over the limbs: 'This breast pressed down
the ravager of Nemea, these arms bore the deadly
club and broke the Argive oars.'
Ah! so great a deceit of form in so small a span!
What measure in the right hand, what experience in the cares
of the learned craftsman, at once to shape an ornament for the table
and to turn over vast colossi in his mind!
Such a thing neither could the Telchines have wrought in their Idaean caves,
nor stupid Brontes, nor the Lemnian who polishes the arms
of the gods, sporting with a scanty mass.
Nor is the image grim and unfitted to relaxed feasts,
but such as the house of frugal Molorchus admired,
or as the Tegean priestess saw in the groves of Alea;
such as he was, sent up to the stars from the Oetaean embers,
when, grim Juno now appeased, he gladly drank the nectar still:
so gentle is his face, as if rejoicing from the heart,
he urges the tables on; this hand holds the drooping
cup of his brother, but this hand remembers the club; the rough seat
he sustains, and the stone with its dressed Nemean covering.
Worthy fortune for the sacred work. The Pellaean
ruler kept the venerable godhead on his glad tables
and carried it as companion of his settings and his risings,
and gladly gave it offerings with the very hand
with which he had taken away and bestowed diadems and overturned
great cities; ever from this he sought spirit for tomorrow's wars,
to this the victor ever told his rich battle-lines,
whether he had dragged the chained Indians from Bromius
or shattered baffled Babylon with his great spear,
or had overwhelmed in war the lands of Pelops and the freedom
of the Pelasgians; and out of the great host of his praises
it is said that he excused only the triumphs over Thebes.
He too, when the Fates were breaking off his great deeds,
as he drained the deadly draught, already heavy
with the dark cloud of death, feared in the dear godhead
other looks, and the bronze sweating at his last feast.
Soon the wondrous ornament was possessed by the Nasamonian king;
and to the brave god there ever paid honours,
savage with his right hand and proud of his perjured sword,
Hannibal. But the god hated him, drenched with the blood of the Italian race
and carrying dread fires to the roofs of Romulus,
both when he set out his feasts and when he dedicated the gifts
of Lenaeus; the god went mourning, a comrade to his accursed camp,
chiefly when with sacrilegious torch he mingled the citadels
of innocent Saguntum, its very homes, and polluted its temples,
and loosed honourable furies upon the peoples.
Nor, after the death of the Sidonian leader, when a plebeian house
possessed the noble bronze, did it cease to adorn the banquets
of Sulla, accustomed ever to enter the houses of the illustrious,
and a sign happy in the lineage of its masters.
Now too, if it is the gods' care to know the ways
and hearts of men: no court, Tirynthian, encloses you,
nor royal honour, but the chaste mind of its lord,
ignorant of guilt, in whom is ancient faith and the perpetual
bond of friendship begun; he knows still, in his flower of life,
Vestinus, equal to his great forebears, whom night and day
he breathes, and lives in the embrace of the dear shade.
Here, then, you have glad peace, bravest of the gods,
Alcides, and you see no wars nor fierce battles,
but the lyre and the fillets and the laurels that love song.
Here in a solemn song he will tell you how great
you terrified the Trojan and Getic homes, how great the snowy
Stymphalus, how great Erymanthus on its watery ridges,
what you were to the master of the Iberian flock,
what to the Maeotian arbiter of the savage altar.
Here he will sing of the thresholds of death, pierced and despoiled by you,
and of the weeping girls of Libya and Scythia.
Neither the ruler of the Macedonians nor barbarian
Hannibal ever, nor the harsh voice of savage Sulla,
could celebrate you in these strains; surely you, the giver of the gift,
would not wish to be approved by other eyes, Lysippus.

Birthday Poem for Lucan, addressed to Polla Let whoever, on the hills of Isthmian Dione, his breast roused by the learned frenzy, drinks the liquor of the hanging hoof, keep Lucan's own day. You yourselves, with whom the honour of singing rests, the Arcadian inventor of the tuneful lyre, and you, Euhan, whirler of the Bassarids, and Paean, and the Hyantian sisters, joyfully renew your purple fillets, deck your hair, and let fresher ivy drench your white robes. Let the learned streams wander more freely, and let the Aonian woods be greener, and, if any shade lies open or has caught the daylight, let it be filled with soft garlands. Let a hundred fragrant altars stand in the Thespian groves, and a hundred victims which Dirce washes or Cithaeron rears: we sing Lucan; keep holy silence, this is your day; favour us, Muses, while he who bore you through the twin arts, both of the bound and the loosened foot of speech, is honoured, the priest of the Roman choir. Happy—alas, too happy!—and blessed land, you who see the downward course of Hyperion in the highest waves of Ocean and hear the whirr of the falling wheel, who, fertile, challenge Tritonian Athens with your oiled presses, Baetica: you can charge Lucan to the earth's account! This is more than to have given Seneca to the world or to have begotten sweet Gallio. Let Baetis, nobler than Greek Meles, lift his back-flowing fountains to the stars; Mantua, do not dare to challenge Baetis. The new-born child, at once, upon the very ground, sweetly wailing at his first cry, Calliope took into her coaxing bosom, then first, her mourning laid aside and softened, put off the long sorrows of Orpheus, and said: 'O boy dedicated to the Muses, soon to surpass the long-lived bards, you shall move neither rivers nor herds of beasts nor the Getic ash-trees with your quill, but the seven ridges and martial Tiber, and the learned knights and, with eloquent song, the senate purple in their robes; the nocturnal ruins of the Phrygians let others, and the ways of slow-returning Ulysses and the rash ship of Minerva— a track worn by bards—follow: you, dear to Latium and mindful of your race, more boldly bring forth the togaed song. And first, while still in your tender years, you shall play of Hector and the Thessalian chariots and the suppliant gold of mighty Priam, and you shall unlock the seats of the dead, ungrateful Nero shall be brought forth for you in the sweet theatres, and our Orpheus. You shall tell of the impious fires of the guilty lord wandering over the roofs of Remus. Hence in a joyful address you shall give the title and honour of chaste Polla. Soon, more nobly in your full youth, you shall thunder of Philippi white with Italian bones and the wars of Pharsalia, and the divine leader convulsed amid arms, and Cato grave with pious freedom, and Magnus, dear in his popularity. You, pious, shall weep the crime of Pelusian Canopus, and to Pompey on bloody Pharos you shall give a loftier tomb. These things you shall sing, a youth in your first age, before the years of the Maronian Gnat. The rude Muse of fierce Ennius shall yield, and the lofty madness of learned Lucretius, and he who led the Argonauts through the straits, and he who transfigures the first bodies. What greater thing shall I say? The very Aeneid shall revere you as you sing to the Latins. Nor shall I give only the splendour of songs, but with the genial torches I shall dedicate to you one learned and graced by your own genius, such as coaxing Venus and Juno would give in form, in simplicity, in courtesy, in wealth, in blood, in grace, in beauty; and before your doors I myself shall sound the wedding-hymn with festive songs. O Fates, too savage and too grievous! O long lives never granted to the highest! Why, lofty things, do you lie more open to disasters? Why do great things not grow old by a savage law? So the son of the Nasamonian Thunderer, after his risings and his thunderstruck settings, narrow Babylon presses in a cramped tomb. So Thetis shuddered at the Pelid, fixed by the hand of raging Paris, as he fell. So I followed along the banks of murmuring Hebrus the not-silent head of Orpheus. So you too—crime of a mad tyrant!—bidden to go down headlong into Lethe, while you sing of battles and with lofty voice give consolation to the great tombs, —O dire wickedness! O wickedness!—shall be silent.' So she spoke, and lightly with her gleaming quill wiped away the falling tears. But you, whether raised aloft on the lofty chariots of Fame through the swift axis of the sky, where the mightier souls rise, look down on the lands and laugh at the tombs; or whether, happy, you hold the grove of unbarred peace, deservedly, on the shores of Elysium, where the Pharsalian throng gathers, and the Pompeys and the Catos accompany you as you sound your noble song; or whether, sacred and proud in your great shade, you know Tartarus and from afar hear the lashes of the guilty and look back upon pale Nero at the sight of his mother's torch: be present, shining, and at Polla's call win, I pray, one day from the gods of the silent; this threshold is wont to open for husbands returning to their brides. She, not wanton, clothes you in no deceiving shape of a false power with her revels, but cherishes you yourself and frequents yourself, set deeper in her inmost marrow, and your face supplies vain solace, the face which, marked in like gold, shines above her bed and broods upon the sleep of the untroubled woman. Far hence depart, you Deaths: this is the origin of genial life. Let cruel grief give way, and on her cheeks now flow sweet tears, and a festive sorrow; whatever she had wept before, now let her adore.
pr. Statius to his Pollius, greeting.

To you at least, sweetest Pollius—and most worthy of that repose to which you cling so faithfully—I have no need to commend at length the boldness of these little books, since you know that many of them were born suddenly in your own bosom, and have often dreaded this audacity of my pen, as often as, drawn aside into the sanctuary of your own eloquence, I go more deeply into letters and am led by you into every recess of study. Secure, therefore, this third book of our Silvae is sent to you. The second indeed had you as its witness, but this one has you as its author. For Hercules of Surrentum opens its first threshold—the Hercules consecrated on your shore, whom, as soon as I had seen him, I worshipped in these verses. There follows the little book in which I thus escorted the most splendid and to me most delightful young man, Maecius Celer, sent by our most sacred Emperor to the Syrian legion, since I could not follow him. The devotion of my Claudius Etruscus, too, deserved some consolation from our studies, while he mourned his aged father with true tears—which is now a most rare thing. Earinus, moreover, the freedman of our Germanicus—you know how long I delayed my response to his desire—when he had asked that I dedicate in verse his hair, which he was sending in a doubled casket, with a mirror, to the Pergamene Asclepius. The last is the eclogue in which I urge my own Claudia to retire with me to Naples. Here, if I speak truly, is conversation, and indeed unguarded, as with a wife, and one who would rather persuade than please. To this little book in particular you will show favour, since you know that this resolve for my repose is aimed especially at you, and that I am retiring not so much to my homeland as to you. Farewell.
A Lyric Ode to Vibius Maximus Now long sated with the broad field,
brave Erato, defer the heroic labours
and contract the vast work into smaller
circuits;
and you, ruler of the lyric band,
grant me a little of the new quill's rights,
if in Latin song I have hallowed
your Thebes, Pindar:
I attempt to make my song slender for Maximus;
now from the unshorn myrtle the garlands
must be taken, now a greater thirst, and a chaster
stream must be drunk.
When will the Dalmatian mountains send you back
to sweet Latium, where, Dis once seen,
the pale miner returns, the colour
of the gold he has dug out?
Behold, though I was born in a nearer land,
yet no pleasant harbour holds me,
nor idle Baiae, nor the trumpeter known
for the arms of Hector.
There is sluggishness in my Camenae without you,
the lord of Thymbra himself comes more slowly
than is his wont, and behold, my Achilles
sticks at the first turning-posts.
For with you as my faithful adviser our
Thebaid, much tortured by the file,
assays with bold string the joys
of Mantuan fame.
But I grant indulgence to your delay, because with kindly
offspring you have founded an empty household,
O happy day! behold, there comes to us
another Maximus!
Childlessness, to be fled with every effort,
which the hostile heir presses with his prayers,
demanding—shame on it, alas!—of his best
friend a kinsman's funeral.
Childlessness, entombed with no weeping:
the greedy survivor stands in the captured house,
hanging over the spoils of death and reckoning
even the funeral fire.
May the noble infant last long,
and along the road open to not many
grow into his father's ways, and challenge
his grandsire by his deeds!
You will recall to the little one your own swords,
which you bore to the Eastern Orontes,
commanding the standards of a bridled squadron
with Castor at your right;
how, following the swift thunderbolt
of unconquered Caesar, you gave the recoiling
Sarmatian the bitter law, to live
beneath a single sky.
But let the boy first learn your arts,
you who, having measured all the world's age,
give back the beginnings of brief Sallust
and the foster-child of Timavus.
A Congratulation to Julius Menecrates Open the doors of the gods and fill the garlanded temples
with Sabaean clouds and the breathing entrails of cattle,
Parthenope; behold, a third offspring now increases
the famous race of bright Menecrates. The noble throng of nobles
grows for you and consoles the losses of mad Vesuvius.
Nor let secret Naples alone surround the festal altars:
let the allied harbour too, and the land entered by levy,
the Dicaearchean shore, and the region dear to the dripping
god of Surrentum, gird its altars with garlands,
where lies the shore of his mother's grandsire, whom the throng of grandsons
surrounds and strives to render in like features,
and let the great-uncle rejoice, distinguished by his Libyan spear,
and Polla, who thinks them her own children and lifts them up
in her kindly lap. Blessing on you, young man, who give such
lights to your deserving country; behold, with sweet tumult trembles
the house acclaimed by so many young masters; far off let black
Envy withdraw and turn its livid heart elsewhere:
to these, old age and the glory of long virtue, and white
Atropos and your father Apollo with his laurel have promised.
Therefore, that the most august father of the Ausonian city
had given you the glad right of threefold offspring,
was an omen. So often Lucina came and entered
your pious home, returning again; so fruitful, I pray,
let the house stand, and never changed in its sacred gifts.
Blessing on you, that your offspring too was more often increased with manly
strength, but a daughter too is to be rejoiced in by a young father
—virtue is fitter for these, but she will give grandchildren sooner—,
such as Helen, now worthy of her mother's wrestling-schools,
crawled, gleaming white, among her Amyclaean brothers;
or such as the face of heaven, when on a serene night
two stars have brought their radiance near the central moon.
But I complain, rarest of young men, with no easy complaints,
and I am even angry, so far as lovers are angry,
that such great joys it was fitting for me to learn from common
rumour? And while your third infant cried,
no letter came at once, a messenger in great haste,
to bid me heap the festal fires upon the altars
and wreathe my lyre and adorn my doorposts
and bring forth a heaven darkened with Alban smoke
and mark the day with song; but slow and idle
do I now at last sing my vows? Yours is the fault and yours
this shame; but to draw out my complaints further
is not permitted; behold, the glad throng of your children stands round
and defends their father—whom would you not conquer with this array?
Native gods, whom over the seas with great auguries
the Abantian fleet brought down to the Ausonian shore;
you, leader of the people in their long migration, Apollo,
whose bird, still seated on her left shoulder,
happy Eumelis, looking back, fondly adores;
and you, Attic Ceres, for whom with breath ever panting
we silent initiates shake the votive torch;
and you, sons of Tyndareus, whom no dread Lycurgan
Taygetus and shady Therapnae honoured more:
these with their people, native gods, preserve, my household gods;
let there be those who may aid with voice and wealth the city
worn out by age and frequent toils, and keep it in a green name.
To these let the father show gentle manners and the grandfather
a generous splendour, each a zeal for fair virtue,
since both their wealth and their birth permit this one with his first torch
to enter the patrician doors, these in their very boyhood,
if only the powers of unconquered Caesar be present,
favourable to the good, to knock at the threshold of the Romulean senate.
Playful Hendecasyllables to Plotius Grypus This is indeed a fine jest, that you have sent
me a little book, Grypus, in return for a little book,
yet it might seem witty,
if after this you send me back something more;
for if you persist in playing, Grypus,
you do not play—come, look, let us reckon it up!
My book, purple and new in its paper
and adorned with two bosses,
cost me, besides myself, ten asses:
you, a thing gnawed by moths and rotten with mould,
such as either drip with Libyan olives
or store Nilotic incense and pepper
or keep the mackerel of Byzantium,
not even containing your own speeches,
which as a young man you thundered in the threefold Forum
or before nearly a hundred judges, before
Germanicus made you arbiter of the following
year's corn-supply and set you in charge, far and wide,
of all the stations of the roads,
but the yawnings of old Brutus,
bought from the box of some wretched bookseller
for more or less a Gaian as,
you give. Was there so utter a lack
of caps stitched from cut cloaks,
or towels, or grimy napkins,
papers, Theban or Carian figs?
Nowhere a ball of plums and Syrian damsons
stored in a tumbling whirl?
No dry lamp-wicks, no folded
skins of onions? Not eggs even,
nor smooth spelt-grits, nor coarse meal?
Nowhere a moist house of curved snails
wandered from the Cinyphian fields?
No heavy bacon or weak ham?
No Lucanian sausage, no heavy Faliscan,
no salt or relish or cheese,
or cakes of green natron,
or raisin-wine from its own grapes recooked,
or new-must muddy with sweet dregs?
What it would not cost even to give scented tapers,
a little knife, or thin writing-tablets?
Were you not allowed, I ask, to give jarred grapes,
dishes turned on a Cuman wheel,
or one dinner-set—why do you shudder?—
of white cups and cooking-pots?
But, like a fair judge with steady balance,
you change nothing, but pay me back the same.
What if, when early in the morning, half-awake,
I have wished you the greeting brought to you,
you too should greet me in turn at home?
Or, when you have helped me with a rich feast,
you yourself should expect like dinners?
I am angry with you, Grypus, but you will fare well;
only do not send me back, with that charm
you are wont to use, even now these hendecasyllables.

Good examples should be honoured with every feeling, since they benefit the public. The devotion you show to your Priscilla is both a part of your character and can win you the goodwill of everyone, above all of a husband. For to love a living wife is a pleasure, a dead one a religious duty. Yet I have not rushed to this work as one of the crowd, nor merely as one performing a service. For Priscilla loved my wife, and by loving her made her more approved in my eyes; after this I should be ungrateful if I passed over your tears. Besides, I strive in my modest way always to deserve well of every quarter of the divine house. For he who worships the gods in good faith loves their priests too. But although I had long desired a closer enjoyment of your friendship, I would rather not yet have found the occasion.
